chapters.title: Loss, Grief and End of Life Care

members.title: Loss, Grief and End of Life Care
Loss, Grief and End of Life Care

questions.stem: Match each loss to its type.

rows.text: A sudden job loss after a plant closes
Amputation of a leg below the knee
Feeling less valued after retiring from a long held role
Children leaving home as an expected life transition
An unexpected cancer diagnosis

questions.takeaway: An actual loss can be seen and recognized by others, such as an amputation or a death. A perceived loss is felt by the person but less obvious to others, such as feeling less valuable after losing a role. A necessary or developmental loss comes with expected life transitions. A situational loss comes from a sudden, unexpected event. One event can involve several types. Actual is visible, perceived is felt, developmental is expected, situational is sudden.
questions.strategy: Ask whether others can see the loss and whether it was expected.

questions.stem: Match each term to its definition.

rows.text: The outward, culturally shaped expression of loss
The internal emotional response to loss
The state of having lost someone

questions.takeaway: Grief is the inner emotional response. Mourning is the outward expression, shaped by culture, such as rituals and customs. Bereavement is the state of having lost someone. Knowing the difference keeps the nurse from judging grief by visible behavior. Grief inside, mourning outside, bereavement the state.
questions.strategy: Separate what is felt from what is shown.

questions.stem: Match each situation to the grief experience it describes.

rows.text: A spouse caring for a partner whose dementia has changed who they are
A family grieving during hospice care before the death occurs
A former partner whose loss is not acknowledged at the funeral
The family of a person who has been missing for months

questions.takeaway: Anticipatory grief begins before an expected loss. Disenfranchised grief is grief that receives little recognition or support, such as an unacknowledged relationship. Ambiguous loss involves uncertainty about absence or presence, such as a missing person or profound change with dementia. These experiences can overlap. Before, unrecognized, uncertain.
questions.strategy: Ask what makes the grief different: its timing, its recognition or its certainty.

questions.stem: Which statement about the five stages of grief is correct?

options.text: Responses can overlap, recur or occur in any order
options.rationale: Denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance describe common responses, not required steps. They can overlap, recur or occur in any order.

options.text: Acceptance means the person no longer feels the loss
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acceptance means beginning to live with the loss and adapting over time.

options.text: Anger is a sign the grief has become complicated
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Anger is a common, normal grief response.

options.text: People must complete each stage in order to heal
options.rationale: Near miss concept The stages are not required steps or a fixed sequence.

questions.takeaway: Stages are not a checklist.
questions.strategy: Reject any option that forces a sequence.

questions.stem: Match each statement to the grief response it reflects.

rows.text: "If I take every treatment, maybe I will live to see the wedding."
"This cannot be right. The scan must belong to someone else."
"I have started planning what I want my last months to look like."
"Why did the doctors miss this for so long? Nobody listened."
"I feel so overwhelmed that I cannot get out of bed."

questions.takeaway: Denial involves disbelief and shock. Anger involves frustration and irritation. Bargaining tries to change the outcome. Depression involves feeling overwhelmed, sad or helpless. Acceptance involves beginning to live with the loss and adapting. Disbelief, blame, deal making, sadness, adapting.
questions.strategy: Listen for the feeling behind the words.

questions.stem: According to attachment theory, why does losing a loved one cause grief?

options.text: The person lacks coping skills learned in childhood
options.rationale: Near miss concept Grief is a normal response, not a skills deficit.

options.text: The loss creates a new attachment that replaces the old one
options.rationale: Near miss concept Adaptation keeps an inner connection rather than replacing it.

options.text: The loss disrupts the safety, comfort and belonging the relationship provided
options.rationale: Close relationships provide safety, comfort and belonging. Losing an attachment figure disrupts that security, which can trigger yearning, searching, anxiety, anger or disbelief. Adaptation means living with the absence while keeping a meaningful inner connection.

options.text: The person has not yet worked through the five stages
options.rationale: Near miss concept Attachment theory explains why loss hurts, not a sequence of stages.

questions.takeaway: Grief is the cost of attachment.
questions.strategy: Find the option about what the relationship provided.

questions.stem: Match each example to Worden's task of mourning.
columns: Accept the reality of the loss
Adjust to life without the deceased
Maintain a connection while moving forward

rows.text: Learning to manage the household finances alone
rows.answer: Adjust to life without the deceased

rows.text: Continuing a family holiday tradition while making new friends
rows.answer: Maintain a connection while moving forward

rows.text: Allowing feelings of sadness, guilt or relief
Gradually realizing the person will not walk through the door again
rows.answer: Accept the reality of the loss

answer.r1: Adjust to life without the deceased
answer.r2: Maintain a connection while moving forward
answer.r4: Accept the reality of the loss

questions.takeaway: Worden's tasks: accept the reality of the loss, process the pain, adjust to life without the deceased and maintain a connection while moving forward. The tasks can overlap and be revisited; they have no fixed order or timeline. Accept, feel, adjust, connect.
questions.strategy: Match the example to what the person is working on.

questions.stem: Classify each activity in the dual process model of grief.

rows.text: Looking through old photographs and crying
Learning to cook meals for the first time
Sharing memories of the person who died
Reconnecting with friends at a weekly club
Taking on a new role at home

questions.takeaway: Loss oriented coping focuses on the person who died and the emotional impact. Restoration oriented coping focuses on managing the life changes the loss caused. People move back and forth between the two, which is called oscillation. Taking breaks and enjoying moments are part of healthy coping. Facing the loss versus rebuilding life.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the activity looks back at the person or forward at daily life.

questions.stem: In the dual process model, what is oscillation?

options.text: Completing all loss coping before starting any restoration coping at all
options.rationale: Near miss concept The model has no fixed sequence.

options.text: Alternating between denial and anger in a fixed pattern
options.rationale: Near miss concept That mixes up the five stages with the dual process model.

options.text: Moving back and forth between facing the loss and adjusting to life
options.rationale: Oscillation is moving between loss oriented and restoration oriented coping, with breaks from each. A grieving person who laughs at a movie one evening is not avoiding grief; this movement is healthy.

options.text: Spending equal time each day on grief and on daily tasks at home
options.rationale: Absolute language The model does not prescribe equal time in each.

questions.takeaway: Oscillation = moving back and forth.
questions.strategy: Reject options that add rules the model does not set.

questions.stem: Complete the statement about Rando's six R processes of mourning.
questions.sentence: The processes are grouped into three phases. Recognizing the death belongs to [[1]]. Reacting, recollecting and relinquishing belong to [[2]]. Readjusting and reinvesting belong to [[3]].

options.text: confrontation
avoidance
accommodation
confrontation
accommodation
avoidance
avoidance
confrontation
accommodation

questions.takeaway: Rando groups the six R processes into avoidance (recognize), confrontation (react, recollect and reexperience, relinquish) and accommodation (readjust, reinvest). Recognize, then confront, then accommodate.
questions.strategy: Place each process by whether the person is acknowledging, feeling or rebuilding.

questions.stem: In Rando's model, what does reinvesting mean?

options.text: Acknowledging that the death has really happened
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is recognize, the first process.

options.text: Remembering the relationship and the feelings it held
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is recollect and reexperience.

options.text: Letting go of expectations that depended on the person being present
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is relinquish.

options.text: Putting emotional energy into relationships, activities and future goals
options.rationale: Reinvest is the last process: putting emotional energy into relationships, activities and future goals while preserving memories.

questions.takeaway: Reinvest is the final R.
questions.strategy: Match the R word to its meaning.

questions.stem: Select all of the factors that shape how a person grieves.

options.text: Previous losses and coping strategies
options.rationale: Grief is shaped by the meaning of the loss, the circumstances, prior losses and coping, available support and resources, and developmental stage, culture and spiritual beliefs. Together these guide individualized assessment.

options.text: A fixed timeline for grief that applies to everyone
options.rationale: Near miss concept Grief has no fixed timeline; responses vary in intensity and change over time.

options.text: The meaning and significance of the relationship
options.rationale: Grief is shaped by the meaning of the loss, the circumstances, prior losses and coping, available support and resources, and developmental stage, culture and spiritual beliefs. Together these guide individualized assessment.

options.text: Whether the death was sudden, traumatic or expected
options.rationale: Grief is shaped by the meaning of the loss, the circumstances, prior losses and coping, available support and resources, and developmental stage, culture and spiritual beliefs. Together these guide individualized assessment.

options.text: The nurse's own beliefs about the right way to grieve
options.rationale: Near miss concept The nurse's beliefs do not shape the patient's grief and should not guide the assessment.

options.text: Culture, spiritual beliefs and developmental stage
options.rationale: Grief is shaped by the meaning of the loss, the circumstances, prior losses and coping, available support and resources, and developmental stage, culture and spiritual beliefs. Together these guide individualized assessment.

questions.takeaway: Many factors shape grief; assess each person.
questions.strategy: Pick factors about the griever.

questions.stem: Select all of the considerations when assessing grief in older adults.

options.text: Changes in housing, finances and routines
options.rationale: Older adults often face multiple concurrent losses that affect housing, finances, routines, transportation and support. Sensory, cognitive and communication needs shape how they are heard. Preserve choices and meaningful roles.

options.text: Older adults grieve less because loss is expected
options.rationale: Near miss concept Expected loss does not mean less grief.

options.text: Several losses may occur at the same time
options.rationale: Older adults often face multiple concurrent losses that affect housing, finances, routines, transportation and support. Sensory, cognitive and communication needs shape how they are heard. Preserve choices and meaningful roles.

options.text: Isolation and limited transportation
options.rationale: Older adults often face multiple concurrent losses that affect housing, finances, routines, transportation and support. Sensory, cognitive and communication needs shape how they are heard. Preserve choices and meaningful roles.

options.text: A single loss at a time, in sequence
options.rationale: Near miss concept Losses often arrive together, not in sequence.

options.text: Sensory, cognitive and communication needs
options.rationale: Older adults often face multiple concurrent losses that affect housing, finances, routines, transportation and support. Sensory, cognitive and communication needs shape how they are heard. Preserve choices and meaningful roles.

questions.takeaway: Older adults: losses stack up.
questions.strategy: Reject stereotypes about older adults.

questions.stem: Which question is the best way to open a grief assessment?

options.text: "What has been hardest for you?"
options.rationale: The assessment begins with what matters most to the person. An open question invites the patient to name the meaning of the loss, and the nurse explores needs without turning it into a rapid checklist. Caregivers are assessed too.

options.text: "Which stage of grief do you think you are in?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Grief is not a fixed sequence of stages.

options.text: "Are you sleeping and eating normally?"
options.rationale: Correct but premature Sleep and nutrition matter, but start with what matters most to the patient.

options.text: "Have you thought about seeing a counselor?"
options.rationale: Correct but premature Referral may come later, after assessment.

questions.takeaway: Start with what is hardest.
questions.strategy: Pick the open question that centers the patient.

questions.stem: Select all of the statements the nurse should avoid with a grieving family.

options.text: "This sounds very painful."
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit This acknowledges the pain and is supportive.

options.text: "Be strong for your children."
options.rationale: Avoid phrases that minimize, dismiss or project feelings. Supportive responses acknowledge pain, offer presence and ask what would help.

options.text: "Don't worry."
options.rationale: Avoid phrases that minimize, dismiss or project feelings. Supportive responses acknowledge pain, offer presence and ask what would help.

options.text: "What would help right now?"
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Asking what would help respects the person's needs.

options.text: "I can sit with you."
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Offering presence is supportive.

options.text: "Everything happens for a reason."
options.rationale: Avoid phrases that minimize, dismiss or project feelings. Supportive responses acknowledge pain, offer presence and ask what would help.

questions.takeaway: Presence beats reassurance.
questions.strategy: In an avoid question, the correct answers are the unhelpful phrases.

questions.stem: What is the best way for the nurse to learn a dying patient's cultural and spiritual preferences?

options.text: Look up the practices of the patient's listed religion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Religion guides questions but does not tell the nurse what this person wants.

options.text: Follow the customs most common in the patient's ethnic group
options.rationale: Near miss concept Assumptions based on group identity can be wrong.

options.text: Ask the chaplain to decide what the patient needs
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope The chaplain supports the plan; the patient sets the preferences.

options.text: Ask the patient what beliefs or practices should be honored
options.rationale: Culture informs care, but the individual defines their own preferences. Ask who should be involved, what beliefs or practices to honor, how to share difficult information and whether spiritual or secular support would help.

questions.takeaway: Ask the person, not the group.
questions.strategy: Avoid assumptions based on identity.

questions.stem: Match each practice to the tradition commonly associated with it. Always confirm with the individual patient and family.

rows.text: Quiet surroundings, chanting or meditation, minimal disturbance
Family led prayers, preserving sacred items, cremation
Positioning toward Mecca, ritual washing, prompt burial
Someone remaining with the deceased, ritual preparation, prompt burial

questions.takeaway: Common practices: Islam, Quran recitation, positioning toward Mecca, ritual washing and prompt burial; Judaism, prayers, someone remaining with the deceased and prompt burial; Hinduism, family led prayers, sacred items and cremation; Buddhism, quiet, chanting and minimal disturbance. These are starting points for questions, not assumptions. Know the practices, then ask the person.
questions.strategy: Use them to guide questions.

questions.stem: A patient has no religious affiliation. Select all of the things that can still provide spiritual support.

options.text: Time in nature
options.rationale: Spiritual support may involve religion, relationships, meaning, nature or personal values. Secular support, such as music or familiar people, is offered when wanted.

options.text: Nothing, since spirituality requires a religion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Spirituality may or may not include religion.

options.text: A sense of meaning or personal values
options.rationale: Spiritual support may involve religion, relationships, meaning, nature or personal values. Secular support, such as music or familiar people, is offered when wanted.

options.text: Relationships with family and friends
options.rationale: Spiritual support may involve religion, relationships, meaning, nature or personal values. Secular support, such as music or familiar people, is offered when wanted.

options.text: Only a hospital chaplain visit
options.rationale: Near miss concept A chaplain can help, but secular sources also support people.

options.text: Meaningful music
options.rationale: Spiritual support may involve religion, relationships, meaning, nature or personal values. Secular support, such as music or familiar people, is offered when wanted.

questions.takeaway: Spirituality is broader than religion.
questions.strategy: Reject options that limit spirituality to religion.

questions.stem: Complete the HOPE mnemonic for spiritual assessment at end of life.
questions.sentence: H stands for sources of [[1]]. O stands for [[2]]. P stands for personal spirituality and practices. E stands for [[3]] of spirituality on care and decisions.

options.text: health
hope and strength
history
organized religion
oxygen needs
outcomes
education
exercise
effects

questions.takeaway: HOPE: sources of hope and strength, organized religion and its role, personal spirituality and practices, and effects of religion and spirituality on care and end of life decisions. Hope, organized religion, personal practices, effects.
questions.strategy: Each blank stands alone.

questions.stem: Classify each statement as palliative care, hospice or both.

rows.text: Can begin at diagnosis alongside curative treatment
Focuses on quality of life and relief of suffering
Requires a prognosis of 6 months or less for adult Medicare eligibility
Includes bereavement support for families after the death
Supports patients and their caregivers

questions.takeaway: Both palliative care and hospice focus on quality of life and relief of suffering and support caregivers. Palliative care fits any stage of serious illness and can accompany curative treatment, with no prognosis requirement. Hospice is a specialized form of palliative care for terminal illness, with a 6 month prognosis for Medicare eligibility and bereavement support for families. All hospice is palliative; not all palliative care is hospice.
questions.strategy: Ask about timing, treatment and eligibility.

questions.stem: Which statement about palliative care is correct?

options.text: It requires a prognosis of 6 months or less
options.rationale: Near miss concept That is a hospice eligibility rule.

options.text: It can begin at diagnosis and accompany curative treatment
options.rationale: Palliative care is specialized support for anyone with serious illness. It focuses on quality of life, symptom relief and the stress of illness, can start at diagnosis, can accompany curative treatment and does not require a 6 month prognosis.

options.text: It is provided only in an inpatient hospice unit
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is offered in hospitals, clinics, homes and other settings.

options.text: It begins only after all treatment has stopped
options.rationale: Near miss concept It can run alongside life prolonging treatment.

questions.takeaway: Palliative care: any stage, any treatment.
questions.strategy: Do not confuse palliative care with hospice.

questions.stem: Select all of the areas a palliative care team addresses.

options.text: Pain, breathlessness, nausea and fatigue
options.rationale: Palliative care addresses physical, emotional, spiritual, social and practical needs and decision support, all centered on the patient's quality of life.

options.text: Curing the underlying disease as the main goal of every visit
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cure is not the focus of palliative care, although curative treatment may continue alongside it.

options.text: Connecting treatment decisions to personal goals
options.rationale: Palliative care addresses physical, emotional, spiritual, social and practical needs and decision support, all centered on the patient's quality of life.

options.text: Meaning, hope and spiritual distress
options.rationale: Palliative care addresses physical, emotional, spiritual, social and practical needs and decision support, all centered on the patient's quality of life.

options.text: Choosing treatments for the patient without asking about goals
options.rationale: Near miss concept Decision support connects options to the patient's goals; the team does not choose for the patient.

options.text: Fear, anxiety and coping with uncertainty
options.rationale: Palliative care addresses physical, emotional, spiritual, social and practical needs and decision support, all centered on the patient's quality of life.

questions.takeaway: Palliative care treats the whole person.
questions.strategy: Pick quality of life domains.

questions.stem: Match each situation to the hospice level of care.

rows.text: Short term intensive support at home during a symptom crisis
Temporary inpatient stay so the usual caregiver can rest
Ongoing support when symptoms are managed without crisis services
Short term care for uncontrolled symptoms that require an inpatient setting

questions.takeaway: Hospice has four levels: routine home care, continuous home care during a crisis, general inpatient care for symptoms that cannot be managed at home and inpatient respite care to give the caregiver a break. Routine, crisis at home, inpatient symptoms, respite.
questions.strategy: Ask where the care happens and why.

questions.stem: Classify each statement about hospice as true or a misconception.

rows.text: Hospice means stopping every treatment
A patient can revoke hospice and may return later if eligible
A patient must have a DNR order to enroll
Hospice is only for patients with cancer
Hospice can continue beyond 6 months with recertification

questions.takeaway: A DNR is not required for hospice, although resuscitation preferences are discussed and documented. Patients can revoke hospice. Other terminal illnesses qualify. Care can continue past 6 months with recertification. Treatment continues when it supports the comfort focused plan. Prognosis is an estimate, not a deadline.
questions.strategy: Watch for absolute claims about hospice.

questions.stem: Which statement about routine home hospice is correct?

options.text: Hospice does not provide any equipment, supplies or medications for the home
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hospice provides equipment, supplies and symptom medications.

options.text: A hospice aide stays continuously at the bedside day and night to give all care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Routine home hospice usually does not supply a continuous caregiver.

options.text: The hospice team makes scheduled visits, and family or others provide daily care
options.rationale: Routine home hospice provides scheduled team visits and access to support. Families, friends, facility staff or paid caregivers usually provide daily hands on care, so the nurse assesses caregiver willingness, ability and health and makes a plan for urgent concerns.

options.text: Hospice nurses give all daily care in the home
options.rationale: Near miss concept Daily hands on care is usually given by family, friends or paid caregivers.

questions.takeaway: Hospice visits; families give daily care.
questions.strategy: Correct the common belief about continuous care.

questions.stem: Match each statement to the document it describes.

rows.text: Can be completed by adults across a range of health statuses
Signed by the patient or decision maker and a physician, NP or PA
Intended for people with serious illness or advanced frailty
Can name a health care agent to make decisions
A medical order that travels with the patient, including into emergency care

questions.takeaway: An advance directive is a legal document that records instructions and can name a health care agent. Adults can complete one at many stages of health. POLST turns treatment preferences into portable medical orders for people with serious illness or advanced frailty, signed by the patient or decision maker and a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant. POLST complements an advance directive; it does not replace it. Advance directive: instructions and an agent. POLST: portable orders.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the document is an order or a statement of wishes.

questions.stem: A patient has an advance directive stating no mechanical ventilation. Is a DNR order now in place?

options.text: No, an advance directive does not automatically create a DNR order
options.rationale: An advance directive records instructions and can name an agent, but it does not automatically create a DNR order. A provider writes the DNR order.

options.text: Yes, if the patient is admitted to a hospital
options.rationale: Near miss concept Admission does not convert the document into an order.

options.text: No, because advance directives are not legal documents in most states
options.rationale: Near miss concept Advance directives are legal documents.

options.text: Yes, an advance directive automatically creates a DNR order
options.rationale: Near miss concept An advance directive records wishes; a DNR is a separate order.

questions.takeaway: Directive is not a DNR order.
questions.strategy: Separate wishes from orders.

questions.stem: A patient has a DNR order and no other limitations. Select all of the care that may continue according to the orders and goals.

options.text: Symptom relief and hygiene
options.rationale: DNR applies after cardiopulmonary arrest. Before arrest, care continues according to the orders and goals. Do not intubate is a separate limitation. DNR does not mean do not treat.

options.text: Emotional support
options.rationale: DNR applies after cardiopulmonary arrest. Before arrest, care continues according to the orders and goals. Do not intubate is a separate limitation. DNR does not mean do not treat.

options.text: Chest compressions after cardiac arrest
options.rationale: Near miss concept A DNR order means resuscitation is not attempted after cardiopulmonary arrest.

options.text: IV fluids
options.rationale: DNR applies after cardiopulmonary arrest. Before arrest, care continues according to the orders and goals. Do not intubate is a separate limitation. DNR does not mean do not treat.

options.text: Oxygen for shortness of breath
options.rationale: DNR applies after cardiopulmonary arrest. Before arrest, care continues according to the orders and goals. Do not intubate is a separate limitation. DNR does not mean do not treat.

options.text: Antibiotics for an infection
options.rationale: DNR applies after cardiopulmonary arrest. Before arrest, care continues according to the orders and goals. Do not intubate is a separate limitation. DNR does not mean do not treat.

questions.takeaway: DNR does not mean do not treat.
questions.strategy: DNR changes what happens after arrest.

questions.stem: When does Section A of the California POLST apply?

options.text: When the patient is admitted to the hospital
options.rationale: Near miss concept Admission does not trigger Section A.

options.text: When the patient can no longer eat or drink
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nutrition preferences are addressed elsewhere.

options.text: When the patient is short of breath but has a pulse
options.rationale: Near miss concept A patient with a pulse is not in arrest; other orders guide care.

options.text: When the patient has no pulse and is not breathing
options.rationale: Section A covers CPR and applies only when the patient has no pulse and is not breathing. The patient chooses either attempt CPR or DNR.

questions.takeaway: Section A = arrest only.
questions.strategy: Match the section to its trigger.

questions.stem: Select all of the correct steps in completing and sharing an advance directive.

options.text: Keep the original locked away where no one can find it
options.rationale: Near miss concept The original must be accessible when needed.

options.text: Give copies to the agent and the health care team
options.rationale: Choose an agent who will honor the wishes and an alternate. California paper directives require a date, signature and witnesses or notarization, with extra protections in skilled nursing facilities. Share copies and keep the original accessible.

options.text: Choose the agent based only on who is the oldest relative
options.rationale: Near miss concept The agent should be someone who will honor the patient's wishes, not chosen by age.

options.text: Sign and date it with witnesses or a notary
options.rationale: Choose an agent who will honor the wishes and an alternate. California paper directives require a date, signature and witnesses or notarization, with extra protections in skilled nursing facilities. Share copies and keep the original accessible.

options.text: Name an alternate agent
options.rationale: Choose an agent who will honor the wishes and an alternate. California paper directives require a date, signature and witnesses or notarization, with extra protections in skilled nursing facilities. Share copies and keep the original accessible.

options.text: Choose an agent who understands and will honor the wishes
options.rationale: Choose an agent who will honor the wishes and an alternate. California paper directives require a date, signature and witnesses or notarization, with extra protections in skilled nursing facilities. Share copies and keep the original accessible.

questions.takeaway: Choose, back up, sign, share.
questions.strategy: Each step makes the directive usable.

questions.stem: When is the best time to start advance care planning conversations?

options.text: Before a crisis, then revisit as health or preferences change
options.rationale: Advance care planning explores values, goals, treatment preferences and who should speak for the patient. It is best started before a crisis and revisited as health or preferences change. Documents record decisions; conversations explain them.

options.text: Only after the provider makes a terminal diagnosis
options.rationale: Near miss concept Planning helps at many stages of health, not only at diagnosis.

options.text: Only once the patient has lost decision making capacity for good
options.rationale: Near miss concept Once capacity is lost, the patient can no longer state wishes.

options.text: During a cardiac arrest, when the decision becomes urgent
options.rationale: Near miss concept A crisis is the worst time to explore values.

questions.takeaway: Plan early, revisit often.
questions.strategy: Choose the option that keeps the patient's voice.

questions.stem: Select all of the abilities that show decision making capacity.

options.text: Agrees with the care team's recommendation
options.rationale: Near miss concept A choice clinicians consider unwise does not establish incapacity.

options.text: Understands the information
options.rationale: Capacity means the patient can understand, appreciate, reason and communicate a choice. A choice clinicians disagree with does not automatically mean incapacity. When uncertain, request assessment and support understanding.

options.text: Reasons about the options
options.rationale: Capacity means the patient can understand, appreciate, reason and communicate a choice. A choice clinicians disagree with does not automatically mean incapacity. When uncertain, request assessment and support understanding.

options.text: Communicates a choice
options.rationale: Capacity means the patient can understand, appreciate, reason and communicate a choice. A choice clinicians disagree with does not automatically mean incapacity. When uncertain, request assessment and support understanding.

options.text: Appreciates the situation and its consequences
options.rationale: Capacity means the patient can understand, appreciate, reason and communicate a choice. A choice clinicians disagree with does not automatically mean incapacity. When uncertain, request assessment and support understanding.

options.text: Is oriented to the date
options.rationale: Near miss concept Orientation alone does not prove or disprove capacity.

questions.takeaway: Understand, appreciate, reason, communicate.
questions.strategy: Capacity is about the process, not agreeing.

questions.stem: A patient cannot make decisions. Place the steps for deciding whose wishes guide care in order.

options.text: If wishes are unknown, consider the patient's values and best interests
Identify the legally authorized decision maker
Follow applicable instructions and known patient wishes

questions.takeaway: First identify the legally authorized decision maker. Then follow the patient's applicable instructions and known wishes. Only if wishes are unknown, consider the patient's values and best interests. The decision maker represents the patient, not personal preferences. Who decides, what the patient wanted, then best interests.
questions.strategy: The patient's own wishes come before anyone else's judgment.

questions.topic: Care during dying and after death
questions.stem: Select all of the steps of postmortem care.
questions.objective: Care during dying and after death

options.text: Insert dentures if the patient wore them
options.rationale: Postmortem care communicates that the person was valued: close the eyes unless a cultural practice says otherwise, insert dentures, straighten the body, put a pillow under the head, place pads and let the family see the patient privately before transfer.

options.text: Place waterproof pads under the hips
options.rationale: Postmortem care communicates that the person was valued: close the eyes unless a cultural practice says otherwise, insert dentures, straighten the body, put a pillow under the head, place pads and let the family see the patient privately before transfer.

options.text: Remove all tubes before asking about an autopsy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tubes stay until it is known whether an autopsy is needed.

options.text: Close the eyes unless a cultural practice calls for a family member to do so
options.rationale: Postmortem care communicates that the person was valued: close the eyes unless a cultural practice says otherwise, insert dentures, straighten the body, put a pillow under the head, place pads and let the family see the patient privately before transfer.

options.text: Transfer the body before the family has seen the patient
options.rationale: Near miss concept Make sure everyone who needs to see the patient has done so.

options.text: Place a pillow under the head
options.rationale: Postmortem care communicates that the person was valued: close the eyes unless a cultural practice says otherwise, insert dentures, straighten the body, put a pillow under the head, place pads and let the family see the patient privately before transfer.

questions.takeaway: Respect, dignity and family time.
questions.strategy: Reject steps done before the autopsy decision or the family's visit.

questions.topic: Care during dying and after death
questions.stem: Which comfort measure is correct for a dying patient with cool, mottled extremities?
questions.objective: Care during dying and after death

options.text: Apply a heating pad to the feet
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heat sources can burn skin with poor circulation.

options.text: Use an electric blanket on high
options.rationale: Near miss concept Electric blankets are avoided.

options.text: Place hot water bottles along the legs
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hot water bottles are avoided.

options.text: Cover the patient with a blanket
options.rationale: Coolness and mottling come from decreased circulation. Cover the patient with a blanket; do not use electric blankets, hot water bottles or heating pads.

questions.takeaway: Cool skin near death: blanket, not heat.
questions.strategy: Protect skin that cannot sense or circulate heat.

questions.stem: Select all of the ways a nurse can cope with repeated patient deaths and prevent burnout.

options.text: Avoid talking about the deaths with anyone
options.rationale: Near miss concept Isolation increases distress.

options.text: Debrief after difficult deaths
options.rationale: Nurses protect their well being through self awareness, healthy coping, debriefing and using available support resources.

options.text: Use workplace support resources
options.rationale: Nurses protect their well being through self awareness, healthy coping, debriefing and using available support resources.

options.text: Build self awareness about personal feelings on death
options.rationale: Nurses protect their well being through self awareness, healthy coping, debriefing and using available support resources.

options.text: Take on extra shifts to stay busy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Overwork increases burnout.

options.text: Practice healthy coping skills
options.rationale: Nurses protect their well being through self awareness, healthy coping, debriefing and using available support resources.

questions.takeaway: Nurses grieve too.
questions.strategy: Pick options that process the loss.

questions.stem: A nurse visits a patient whose spouse died 3 months ago. Classify each finding as a common grief response or one that needs further assessment or referral.

rows.text: Cries when looking at the spouse's photograph
Has stopped eating and lost 18 lb
Says, "I do not see the point of going on anymore"
Has trouble concentrating while reading
Now drinks a bottle of wine every night to sleep
Feels sad, but still goes to a weekly card game

questions.takeaway: Crying, trouble concentrating and sadness alternating with ordinary activities are common responses that ease with time and support. Inability to meet basic needs, severe functional impairment, increasing harmful substance use and hopelessness or thoughts of self harm need further assessment or referral. Grief is normal; danger to basic needs or safety is not.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the finding threatens safety or basic needs.

questions.stem: A patient whose child died 6 weeks ago says, "I do not see the point of anything anymore. Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me." What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Encourage the patient to stay busy with daily activities
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Distraction does not address hopelessness or self harm.

options.text: Reassure the patient that these feelings are a normal part of grief
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Normalizing misses a possible safety risk.

options.text: Ask directly whether the patient is thinking about suicide
options.rationale: Hopelessness and statements about others being better off without them are warning signs. The nurse asks directly about suicidal thoughts, which does not plant the idea, and gets help based on the answer.

options.text: Suggest joining a bereavement support group next month
options.rationale: Correct but premature A support group helps later; safety comes first.

questions.takeaway: Hopelessness in grief: ask about self harm.
questions.strategy: Safety outranks support.

questions.stem: A nurse writes a care plan for a widowed patient who is isolated after a spouse's death. Which outcome is best?

options.text: The patient will identify one person to contact for support by discharge
options.rationale: A good outcome is realistic, patient centered and measurable, and it matches the priority need, here isolation. Identifying one support person is concrete and achievable.

options.text: The patient will complete all five stages of grief
options.rationale: Near miss concept Grief stages are not required steps.

options.text: The patient will understand that grief is a normal process by discharge
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Understand is not measurable.

options.text: The patient will stop feeling sad within 2 weeks
options.rationale: Near miss concept Grief is not a problem to be fixed on a timeline.

questions.takeaway: Outcome: realistic, measurable, tied to the need.
questions.strategy: Reject outcomes that are vague or treat grief as a disease.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from a below the knee amputation says, "Everyone keeps telling me I am lucky to be alive. They do not understand that my whole life has changed." Select all of the losses the nurse should explore.

options.text: Loss of hearing
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing suggests a sensory loss.

options.text: Loss of a family member
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing in the situation suggests a death.

options.text: Changes in future plans
options.rationale: A single event can bring many losses. An amputation can affect function, independence, work, finances, body image and future plans. The nurse assesses pain, daily function, coping, support, finances and safety.

options.text: Changes in body image
options.rationale: A single event can bring many losses. An amputation can affect function, independence, work, finances, body image and future plans. The nurse assesses pain, daily function, coping, support, finances and safety.

options.text: Loss of function and independence
options.rationale: A single event can bring many losses. An amputation can affect function, independence, work, finances, body image and future plans. The nurse assesses pain, daily function, coping, support, finances and safety.

options.text: Loss of work or income
options.rationale: A single event can bring many losses. An amputation can affect function, independence, work, finances, body image and future plans. The nurse assesses pain, daily function, coping, support, finances and safety.

questions.takeaway: One event, many losses.
questions.strategy: Each correct loss follows from the amputation.

questions.stem: A family member sits by a dying patient and says, "I keep thinking I should have brought them to the doctor sooner." Which response is best?

options.text: "Everything happens for a reason, even when we cannot see it."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Philosophical reassurance minimizes the loss.

options.text: "You should not blame yourself; there was nothing you could have done."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic It dismisses the feeling and may not be true.

options.text: "It sounds like you are carrying a lot of guilt. Tell me more."
options.rationale: Reflecting the feeling and inviting the person to say more keeps the focus on them. Avoid phrases that minimize, dismiss or project feelings: don't worry, I know exactly how you feel, be strong, everything happens for a reason.

options.text: "I know exactly how you feel; I went through the very same thing last year."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Claiming to know exactly how someone feels shifts the focus to the nurse.

questions.takeaway: Reflect and invite; do not fix.
questions.strategy: Pick the response that lets the person keep talking.

questions.stem: A dying patient's spouse sits silently and tearful at the bedside. The nurse has no urgent tasks. Which action is most therapeutic?

options.text: Leave the room so the spouse can have privacy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Leaving without asking may feel like abandonment.

options.text: Suggest the spouse go home and rest
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Sending the spouse away overrides what the spouse may want.

options.text: Explain the stages of grief so the spouse knows what to expect
options.rationale: Correct but premature Teaching may help later; right now the need is presence.

options.text: Sit quietly with the spouse and say, "I can sit with you."
options.rationale: Presence is listening and acknowledging the person's loss and pain. Sitting quietly and offering to stay is therapeutic communication without words.

questions.takeaway: Presence is an intervention.
questions.strategy: Pick the option that meets the emotional need now.

questions.stem: A patient has just died. The family has said their faith includes specific practices around the body. What should the nurse do before washing or repositioning the body?

options.text: Begin postmortem care right away to prevent changes in the body
options.rationale: Near miss concept Starting without asking may violate the family's practices.

options.text: Ask the family about practices before touching, washing or moving the body
options.rationale: Ask before touching, washing, repositioning or removing sacred items. Many traditions have specific practices, such as ritual washing or someone remaining with the body. Accommodate requests within safety and legal requirements.

options.text: Remove all sacred items so they are not lost during transfer
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sacred items are not removed without asking.

options.text: Call the funeral home to ask which practices apply to this family and their faith
options.rationale: Near miss concept The family, not the funeral home, knows their practices.

questions.takeaway: Ask before you touch.
questions.strategy: The family's practices come before routine steps.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced heart failure continues treatment but has persistent breathlessness, poor sleep and anxiety. The spouse says they feel overwhelmed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Suggest hospice, since treatment is no longer working
options.rationale: Near miss concept The patient is still receiving treatment; palliative care can accompany it.

options.text: Assess the symptoms and caregiver needs and discuss a palliative care referral
options.rationale: Palliative care fits any stage and can accompany treatment. The nurse assesses symptom severity and function, gives ordered treatment and evaluates it, asks what matters most, identifies caregiver needs and discusses a palliative care referral with the clinician.

options.text: Tell the spouse that feeling overwhelmed is expected and will pass with a little more time
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Normalizing ignores a real caregiver need.

options.text: Increase the diuretic to relieve the breathlessness
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Changing a dose is not a nursing decision.

questions.takeaway: Serious illness plus symptoms: think palliative care.
questions.strategy: Palliative care does not require stopping treatment.

questions.stem: A patient enrolled in hospice 7 months ago is still alive and eligible. The family asks whether hospice will now end. Which response is best?

options.text: "Yes, hospice ends at 6 months, so we will plan a discharge."
options.rationale: Absolute language Six months is an estimate for eligibility, not a maximum.

options.text: "Hospice can continue if the provider recertifies that the patient remains eligible."
options.rationale: For adult Medicare hospice, a physician certifies a prognosis of 6 months or less if the illness follows its usual course. Hospice can continue beyond 6 months with appropriate recertification.

options.text: "The patient must reenroll as a new patient each month."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Recertification, not monthly reenrollment, continues the benefit.

options.text: "Hospice will continue only if the patient agrees to stop all medications."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Medications for comfort continue.

questions.takeaway: Prognosis is an estimate, not a deadline.
questions.strategy: Reject the six month maximum.

questions.stem: A family caring for a patient at home on hospice says they have not slept in days and are exhausted. Which option should the nurse discuss with the hospice team?

options.text: Continuous home care
options.rationale: Near miss concept Continuous home care is for a symptom crisis, not caregiver rest.

options.text: Inpatient respite care
options.rationale: Inpatient respite care is temporary inpatient care that gives the usual caregiver a break. Caregiver strain is part of the hospice plan.

options.text: General inpatient care
options.rationale: Near miss concept General inpatient care is for uncontrolled symptoms.

options.text: Disenrolling from hospice
options.rationale: Near miss concept Leaving hospice removes support the family needs.

questions.takeaway: Exhausted caregiver: respite.
questions.strategy: Match the level of care to the reason.

questions.stem: A patient lacks capacity and has a valid DNR POLST. The patient's adult child says, "I do not care what that paper says. Do everything." What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess the patient and confirm the current documents and orders
options.rationale: Verify first: assess the patient and confirm the applicable documents and current orders. Then acknowledge the distress, clarify whether the child reports a newer patient decision or a personal preference, avoid promising to override the patient, escalate to the clinician and charge nurse and document.

options.text: Tell the adult child the paper cannot be changed and end the conversation
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Dismissing the family's distress damages trust and skips clarification.

options.text: Call a code if the patient arrests, to avoid conflict
options.rationale: Near miss concept Resuscitation against a valid DNR violates the patient's wishes.

options.text: Follow the adult child's request, since family is present
options.rationale: Near miss concept Family disagreement alone does not override the patient's choices.

questions.takeaway: Verify, communicate, escalate, document.
questions.strategy: The patient's documented wishes guide care.

questions.stem: After confirming a valid DNR POLST, the nurse speaks with the patient's adult child, who still wants everything done. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Document that the family is being difficult
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documentation records statements and actions, not labels.

options.text: Promise to talk the provider into changing the order
options.rationale: Near miss concept The nurse avoids promising to override the patient's wishes.

options.text: Acknowledge the distress and ask whether the patient recently expressed a different wish
options.rationale: The nurse acknowledges the distress and clarifies whether the child reports a newer decision by the patient or a personal preference. Then the nurse notifies the clinician and charge nurse, requests ethics, palliative care, social work or spiritual support as needed and documents statements, notifications and care.

options.text: Explain that the family has no role in decisions about the patient's care now
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Family provides important information even without decision authority.

questions.takeaway: Clarify whose wish it is.
questions.strategy: Separate a new patient decision from family preference.

questions.stem: A patient with decision making capacity chooses to stop dialysis. The nurse thinks this decision is unwise. What does this mean for the patient's capacity?

options.text: An unwise choice alone does not establish incapacity
options.rationale: A choice clinicians consider unwise does not automatically establish incapacity. If the patient can understand, appreciate, reason and communicate a choice, the patient decides. When uncertain, the nurse requests an assessment.

options.text: The family must now make the decision
options.rationale: Near miss concept A patient with capacity directs their own care.

options.text: The nurse should delay care until the patient changes the decision
options.rationale: Near miss concept Delaying care to change a decision is coercive.

options.text: The patient lacks capacity
options.rationale: Near miss concept Capacity is about understanding and reasoning, not agreeing.

questions.takeaway: Disagreeing is not incapacity.
questions.strategy: Separate the choice from the ability to choose.

questions.stem: A patient with decision making capacity wants to enroll in hospice. The adult child says, "You are giving up. We want another treatment." What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay hospice until the family agrees
options.rationale: Near miss concept The patient with capacity directs care; family agreement is not required.

options.text: Confirm the patient understands the options
options.rationale: The nurse confirms the patient understands the options, explores the patient's goals and the family's concerns, supports an informed, voluntary decision, involves the treating clinician and support services and documents the discussion and plan.

options.text: Ask the provider to order the new treatment
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope The patient has chosen hospice.

options.text: Tell the adult child the decision is final
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Dismissing the family skips exploring their concerns.

questions.takeaway: Patient with capacity decides; nurse supports.
questions.strategy: Advocate for the informed patient.

questions.topic: Care during dying and after death
questions.stem: A nurse assesses a patient on home hospice. Select all of the findings that suggest death is approaching.
questions.objective: Care during dying and after death

options.text: Cool, mottled extremities
options.rationale: As death nears: Cheyne Stokes respirations, cool and mottled extremities from poor perfusion, death rattle from secretions and a falling, often only palpable, blood pressure. The pulse may speed up, become irregular and weaken.

options.text: A blood pressure that is only palpable
options.rationale: As death nears: Cheyne Stokes respirations, cool and mottled extremities from poor perfusion, death rattle from secretions and a falling, often only palpable, blood pressure. The pulse may speed up, become irregular and weaken.

options.text: A strong, bounding radial pulse
options.rationale: Near miss concept Peripheral circulation weakens as death nears; the pulse becomes weak and irregular.

options.text: Increased appetite and energy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Appetite and energy decrease as death nears.

options.text: Periods of apnea alternating with rapid breathing
options.rationale: As death nears: Cheyne Stokes respirations, cool and mottled extremities from poor perfusion, death rattle from secretions and a falling, often only palpable, blood pressure. The pulse may speed up, become irregular and weaken.

options.text: Loud, wet respirations
options.rationale: As death nears: Cheyne Stokes respirations, cool and mottled extremities from poor perfusion, death rattle from secretions and a falling, often only palpable, blood pressure. The pulse may speed up, become irregular and weaken.

questions.takeaway: Breathing, skin, secretions, sleep, pressure.
questions.strategy: Pick signs of slowing body systems.

questions.topic: Care during dying and after death
questions.stem: A dying patient has loud, gurgling respirations. The family is distressed. What should the nurse do first?
questions.objective: Care during dying and after death

options.text: Increase the oxygen to 6 L/min
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Oxygen does not reduce secretions.

options.text: Perform deep oropharyngeal suctioning
options.rationale: Near miss concept Suctioning is often ineffective and may agitate the patient.

options.text: Reposition the patient onto one side
options.rationale: The death rattle comes from secretions the patient cannot clear. Reposition onto one side, clean the mouth gently and give ordered anticholinergics, such as atropine drops or scopolamine, to dry secretions. Explain to the family what it means.

options.text: Start IV fluids to thin the secretions
options.rationale: Near miss concept IV fluids increase secretions near death.

questions.takeaway: Death rattle: side position, anticholinergic, no deep suction.
questions.strategy: Pick the gentlest effective step.

questions.topic: Care during dying and after death
questions.stem: A patient in hospice has dyspnea with a respiratory rate of 30. SpO2 is 93%. Select all of the appropriate nursing actions.
questions.objective: Care during dying and after death

options.text: Direct a bedside fan toward the face
options.rationale: Opioids such as morphine are the standard treatment for dyspnea near death. A fan toward the face often brings relief. Oxygen is offered for comfort regardless of saturation, usually by nasal cannula because masks can feel frightening. The head of the bed is raised.

options.text: Offer oxygen by nasal cannula for comfort
options.rationale: Opioids such as morphine are the standard treatment for dyspnea near death. A fan toward the face often brings relief. Oxygen is offered for comfort regardless of saturation, usually by nasal cannula because masks can feel frightening. The head of the bed is raised.

options.text: Give low dose morphine as ordered
options.rationale: Opioids such as morphine are the standard treatment for dyspnea near death. A fan toward the face often brings relief. Oxygen is offered for comfort regardless of saturation, usually by nasal cannula because masks can feel frightening. The head of the bed is raised.

options.text: Request intubation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Intubation does not match comfort focused goals.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: Opioids such as morphine are the standard treatment for dyspnea near death. A fan toward the face often brings relief. Oxygen is offered for comfort regardless of saturation, usually by nasal cannula because masks can feel frightening. The head of the bed is raised.

options.text: Hold oxygen because the saturation is above 90%
options.rationale: Near miss concept Oxygen is offered for comfort regardless of the saturation.

questions.takeaway: Dyspnea near death: morphine, fan, oxygen for comfort, head up.
questions.strategy: Comfort is the outcome.

questions.topic: Care during dying and after death
questions.stem: A family asks the nurse to start IV fluids because their dying relative has stopped eating and drinking. Which response is best?
questions.objective: Care during dying and after death

options.text: "We will start fluids right away so the patient does not dehydrate."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fluids near death can increase secretions, nausea and edema.

options.text: "Not wanting food or fluids is expected now, and fluids can add discomfort."
options.rationale: Anorexia near death is expected. Fluids can increase respiratory secretions, nausea, vomiting, edema and ascites. The nurse explains this with sensitivity and offers mouth care, sips or ice chips if the patient can swallow.

options.text: "The patient must eat to stay comfortable, so we will try harder."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Forcing food or fluids is not appropriate.

options.text: "Fluids are not allowed in hospice, so the team cannot start an IV for any reason."
options.rationale: Absolute language This is inaccurate and does not teach.

questions.takeaway: Near death, less intake is normal.
questions.strategy: Teach the family what comfort looks like.

questions.topic: Care during dying and after death
questions.stem: A dying patient becomes restless and agitated. What should the nurse assess first?
questions.objective: Care during dying and after death

options.text: Pain, urinary retention and constipation
options.rationale: Agitation near death first requires assessing for reversible causes: pain, urinary retention and constipation. If these are ruled out, terminal delirium is considered. Calm measures include soft talk, dim lights and low noise; restraints are not used.

options.text: Whether the patient needs an antipsychotic
options.rationale: Correct but premature Drugs come after reversible causes are ruled out.

options.text: Whether visitors should leave
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Removing family does not address the cause.

options.text: Whether the patient needs restraints for safety
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dying patients are not restrained.

questions.takeaway: Agitation: check pain, bladder, bowel first.
questions.strategy: Look for the fixable cause.

questions.topic: Care during dying and after death
questions.stem: A patient expected to die is on home hospice. The family calls to say the patient has stopped breathing. What should the nurse tell the family?
questions.objective: Care during dying and after death

options.text: Call the hospice service
options.rationale: For an expected death at home, 911 is not called. The family calls the hospice service, and the nurse or provider pronounces death per state law and agency policy.

options.text: Begin CPR until help arrives
options.rationale: Near miss concept CPR is not attempted in an expected hospice death.

options.text: Call the medical examiner
options.rationale: Near miss concept The medical examiner is notified for unexpected or suspicious deaths.

options.text: Call 911 right away
options.rationale: Near miss concept 911 is not called for an expected home death.

questions.takeaway: Expected home death: call hospice.
questions.strategy: Match the call to the type of death.

questions.topic: Care during dying and after death
questions.stem: A patient has just died in the hospital. No autopsy is planned. Place the nurse's postmortem actions in order.
questions.objective: Care during dying and after death

options.text: Attach identification tags and prepare for transfer
Ask the family whether they want to help wash the patient or spend time first
Confirm with the provider whether an autopsy is needed
Remove tubes and lines per agency policy

questions.takeaway: Before removing anything, confirm whether an autopsy is required. Offer the family time and the chance to help, honoring cultural practices. If no autopsy is planned, remove tubes and lines per policy, then prepare the body and attach identification tags for transfer. Autopsy question first, family time next, then preparation.
questions.strategy: Never remove lines before the autopsy decision.

questions.stem: A spouse caring for a patient on home hospice says, "I do not know what to do if the patient is in pain at night." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Suggest the spouse sleep in another room
options.rationale: Near miss concept This does not address managing symptoms.

options.text: Tell the spouse to call 911 at night
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hospice provides an after hours plan; 911 is not the plan for expected symptoms.

options.text: Develop a clear plan for symptoms, medication questions and urgent concerns
options.rationale: Families provide most daily hospice care. The nurse assesses the caregiver's willingness and ability and creates a clear plan for symptoms, medication questions and urgent concerns, including whom to call.

options.text: Reassure the spouse that pain rarely happens at night, so there is no need for a plan
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic False reassurance leaves the caregiver unprepared.

questions.takeaway: Prepared caregivers cope better.
questions.strategy: Choose the option that equips the caregiver.

questions.stem: A nurse who cared for a patient for three weeks is found crying in the medication room after the patient's death. What should the charge nurse do first?

options.text: Refer the nurse to the employee assistance program
options.rationale: Correct but premature A referral helps if grief is prolonged or interferes with work, but support comes first.

options.text: Reassign the nurse away from dying patients for the rest of the week
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Well meant, but it treats normal grief as a problem.

options.text: Remind the nurse that professional boundaries prevent this kind of grief
options.rationale: Near miss concept Grief after a patient's death is a normal response, not a boundary violation.

options.text: Acknowledge the loss and offer time to talk or a team debriefing
options.rationale: Nurses grieve too. Normal grief is acknowledged, not avoided. Immediate support, a moment away and a debriefing help the nurse process the loss. Formal referral is for grief that persists or impairs functioning.

questions.takeaway: Nurse grief: acknowledge and debrief first.
questions.strategy: Choose support before referral.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced cancer and decision making capacity asks, "Am I dying?" Earlier, the family asked the nurse not to discuss dying with the patient. What is the best response?

options.text: "What have you noticed that makes you ask that today?"
options.rationale: The patient with capacity has the right to information. The nurse first explores what the patient already senses and wants to know, which keeps the conversation open and honest. The answer then guides who should share the prognosis and how.

options.text: "Your family wants us to focus on keeping you comfortable."
options.rationale: Institution as rationale The family's request does not override the patient's right to information.

options.text: "I can't answer that, but I can ask your provider to come talk with you."
options.rationale: Correct but premature Involving the provider may follow, but first learn what the patient knows and wants.

options.text: "You are very sick, but everyone here is doing everything we can."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Reassurance closes the conversation the patient opened.

questions.takeaway: "Am I dying?": explore first.
questions.strategy: Open the conversation before handing it off.

questions.stem: Eighteen months after a spouse's death, a patient still cannot enter the bedroom, has stopped seeing friends and says, "Nothing matters anymore." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Encourage the patient to begin clearing out the bedroom slowly
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question It addresses one behavior and misses the risk.

options.text: Ask directly about thoughts of self harm and refer for further evaluation
options.rationale: Intense grief that persists beyond a year with withdrawal and hopelessness suggests prolonged grief and possible depression. A statement like "nothing matters" requires a direct question about suicide, then referral.

options.text: Reassure the patient that grief has no timeline and will ease with time
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Grief has no deadline, but hopelessness and withdrawal at this point need assessment.

options.text: Suggest a bereavement support group that meets weekly
options.rationale: Correct but premature A group may help after safety is assessed.

questions.takeaway: Prolonged grief with hopelessness: ask about suicide.
questions.strategy: Safety before support.

questions.stem: A patient with capacity is from a culture in which serious news is traditionally shared with the family first. The provider needs to discuss new test results. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Follow the cultural practice and share the results with the family first
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism A cultural pattern does not decide for this patient.

options.text: Share the results with the patient alone to protect confidentiality
options.rationale: Absolute language The patient may want family present; assuming either way skips the patient.

options.text: Ask the family how they would like the results to be shared
options.rationale: Near miss concept The family does not decide for a patient with capacity.

options.text: Ask the patient how information should be shared and with whom
options.rationale: Culture informs care, but the individual defines their preferences. The nurse asks the patient how and with whom information should be shared and then honors that choice, which may include family first.

questions.takeaway: Ask the person, not the culture.
questions.strategy: The patient with capacity sets the plan.

questions.stem: A nursing home resident has a POLST marked comfort measures only. After a fall, the resident has a deformed hip and severe pain that the available medications do not control. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Call the family to decide whether the resident should go to the hospital
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope The POLST already states the resident's wishes.

options.text: Arrange transfer to the hospital for comfort care
options.rationale: Comfort measures only means treatment is aimed at relief, not cure. The POLST allows transfer to the hospital when comfort cannot be achieved in the current setting, such as for a fracture with uncontrolled pain.

options.text: Keep the resident in the facility, since comfort measures only means no transfer
options.rationale: Absolute language Comfort measures allow transfer when comfort cannot be met where the resident is.

options.text: Give the maximum dose of the available analgesic and reassess in four hours
options.rationale: Correct but premature Waiting four hours with uncontrolled pain fails the comfort goal.

questions.takeaway: Comfort only can still mean transfer, for comfort.
questions.strategy: Read what the order is for, not only what it limits.

questions.stem: Select all of the instructions for a patient receiving external beam radiation.

options.text: Apply powder or deodorant to the area to reduce moisture
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nothing goes on the field unless the radiation team approves it; powder cakes in skin folds. The old aluminum worry has not held up, so ask rather than assume a ban.

options.text: Wash the area gently with mild soap and water only
options.rationale: External beam radiation does not make the patient radioactive, so no isolation is needed, and that misconception causes real distress and social withdrawal. The skin care is gentle washing, nothing applied unless prescribed, no friction and lifelong sun protection, because that skin never fully recovers. Isolation belongs to internal radiation.

options.text: Do not remove the skin markings
options.rationale: External beam radiation does not make the patient radioactive, so no isolation is needed, and that misconception causes real distress and social withdrawal. The skin care is gentle washing, nothing applied unless prescribed, no friction and lifelong sun protection, because that skin never fully recovers. Isolation belongs to internal radiation.

options.text: Protect the area from sun exposure for life

options.rationale: Near miss concept The vaccine prevents infection with a virus that causes cancer. That is risk reduction, not screening.

options.text: A yearly fecal immunochemical stool test
options.rationale: This looks for hidden blood from colon cancer in a person without symptoms, which is screening. Low dose CT finds lung cancer early in a high risk person without symptoms, which is screening. A routine skin check looks for skin cancer early in a person without symptoms, which is screening.

options.text: Wearing sunscreen outdoors
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sunscreen lowers the chance of skin cancer starting. That is risk reduction.

options.text: A yearly low dose chest CT after years of heavy smoking
options.rationale: This looks for hidden blood from colon cancer in a person without symptoms, which is screening. Low dose CT finds lung cancer early in a high risk person without symptoms, which is screening. A routine skin check looks for skin cancer early in a person without symptoms, which is screening.

options.text: A biopsy of a mole that changed color
options.rationale: Near miss concept A biopsy works up a finding that already exists. That is diagnostic evaluation, not screening.

options.text: A monthly skin check for new or changing moles
options.rationale: This looks for hidden blood from colon cancer in a person without symptoms, which is screening. Low dose CT finds lung cancer early in a high risk person without symptoms, which is screening. A routine skin check looks for skin cancer early in a person without symptoms, which is screening.

questions.takeaway: Screening finds cancer early in people without symptoms. Risk reduction stops cancer from starting, and diagnostic evaluation works up a finding.
questions.strategy: For each option ask: does it prevent cancer, look for it in a well person, or work up a finding? Only the middle group is screening.

questions.topic: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage
questions.stem: A patient with a small breast tumor, T1 N0 M0, grade 3, asks why chemotherapy is recommended when the tumor is so small. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage

options.text: “Grade 3 cells look very abnormal and tend to grow and spread faster.”
options.rationale: Grade describes how abnormal the cells look. Poorly differentiated, grade 3 cells are aggressive, so treatment may be advised even when the stage is early.

options.text: “A small tumor always needs chemotherapy before surgery.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Tumor size alone does not require chemotherapy, and the absolute “always” is inaccurate.

options.text: “Grade 3 means the cancer is already in three lymph nodes.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Grade is not about lymph nodes. N0 means no nodes are involved.

options.text: “Your cancer has already spread, so the size of the tumor no longer matters at all.”
options.rationale: Absolute language M0 means no distant spread was found. The stage is early.

questions.takeaway: Stage (TNM) tells how far the cancer has spread; grade tells how abnormal and aggressive the cells are. A high grade can change treatment even at an early stage.
questions.strategy: The TNM part is reassuring, so the reason for chemotherapy must come from the grade. Reject options that confuse grade with nodes or spread.

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: After surgery removed a colon tumor with clear margins, a patient asks, “Why do I need chemotherapy if the cancer is gone?” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

options.text: “Chemotherapy will shrink the tumor before your surgery.”
options.rationale: Correct but premature Chemotherapy before surgery to shrink a tumor is neoadjuvant. This patient's surgery is already done.

options.text: “Chemotherapy is only to keep you comfortable now.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Comfort focused treatment is palliative. This chemotherapy aims to prevent the cancer from coming back.

options.text: “It kills cancer cells that may remain but are too small to detect.”
options.rationale: This is adjuvant chemotherapy: given after the main treatment to destroy hidden cells and lower the chance of recurrence.

options.text: “Clear margins mean the surgeon was not able to remove all of the cancer cells.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Clear margins mean no cancer was seen at the edges of the removed tissue, which is the goal of surgery.

questions.takeaway: Adjuvant therapy follows surgery to kill undetected cells and prevent recurrence. Neoadjuvant therapy comes before surgery to shrink the tumor.
questions.strategy: Timing decides the name: the surgery is done, so the treatment is adjuvant, and its job is to catch what cannot be seen.

questions.topic: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads
questions.stem: A patient is told a lump on the back is a lipoma, a benign tumor, and asks, “Can it spread to other organs?” Which response is accurate?
questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

options.text: “It stays in one place, but it can press on nearby structures.”
options.rationale: Benign cells grow in the wrong place or at the wrong time but stay localized. They do not invade or metastasize, yet a growing mass can still press on nerves or organs.

options.text: “It can spread, but much more slowly than a cancer.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Benign tumors do not spread at all. Slow spread is not a feature of a benign tumor.

options.text: “It cannot spread, so it will never cause any problems.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Benign tumors can still cause problems by pressure or by their size, so “never” is wrong.

options.text: “It will turn into a cancer over time if it is not removed soon.”
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic A benign tumor is a separate kind of growth. It does not routinely become malignant.

questions.takeaway: Benign tumors stay localized and do not invade or spread, but they can press on nearby structures. Malignant cells invade and metastasize.
questions.strategy: Separate spread from harm: benign means no spread, not no harm. Reject the option that claims spread and the one with an absolute.

questions.topic: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads
questions.stem: A patient starting bevacizumab, a drug that blocks angiogenesis, asks how it fights the tumor. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

options.text: “It kills every fast dividing cell in your body.”
options.rationale: Absolute language That describes traditional chemotherapy. Bevacizumab acts on blood vessel growth, not on all dividing cells.

options.text: “It helps your immune system recognize the cancer.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept That describes immunotherapy. Bevacizumab does not act on the immune system.

options.text: “It blocks the new blood vessels the tumor needs to grow.”
options.rationale: Tumors larger than a few millimeters must grow their own blood supply, a process called angiogenesis. Blocking it starves the tumor of oxygen and nutrients.

options.text: “It repairs the damaged genes inside each of the cancer cells in your body.”
