options.rationale: Near miss concept Current drug repairs the gene changes in cancer cells. This is a common misconception.

questions.takeaway: Angiogenesis lets a tumor build its own blood supply so it can keep growing and spread. Drugs that block it slow tumor growth.
questions.strategy: Name the process in the stem, angiogenesis, then match each option to the therapy it really describes.

questions.topic: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads
questions.stem: A patient treated for colon cancer 2 years ago has a lung nodule showing colon cancer cells and asks, “So now I have lung cancer too?” Which response is accurate?
questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

options.text: “It is colon cancer that has spread to the lung.”
options.rationale: A tumor is named for the tissue it started in. Colon cells that traveled through blood or lymph and formed a new colony in the lung are metastatic colon cancer.

options.text: “Yes, the lung tumor is a new and separate cancer.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept A new primary lung cancer would be made of lung cells. The biopsy shows colon cells, so this is spread.

options.text: “It is a benign growth caused by the earlier treatment.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The biopsy shows cancer cells, so the growth is malignant, not benign.

options.text: “The colon cancer turned into lung cancer as it spread.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cancer cells keep their tissue of origin when they spread. They do not change into lung cancer.

questions.takeaway: Metastatic tumors keep the name of the primary cancer: colon cells in the lung are metastatic colon cancer, not lung cancer.
questions.strategy: Let the biopsy decide. The cell type tells you where the cancer started, wherever it is found.

questions.topic: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage
questions.stem: The nurse reviews the diagnoses of six patients on an oncology unit. For each diagnosis, indicate how the tumor is classified.
questions.objective: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage

rows.text: Liposarcoma of the thigh
Lipoma on the shoulder
Adenocarcinoma of the colon
Osteoma of the skull
Osteosarcoma of the femur
Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin

questions.takeaway: A malignant tumor of fat, which is connective tissue, is a sarcoma. The ending “oma” without carcinoma or sarcoma usually names a benign tumor; “lipo” means fat. Carcinomas arise from epithelial tissue; “adeno” means glandular epithelium. Osteoma is a benign bone tumor; the malignant version is osteosarcoma. Sarcomas arise from connective tissue such as bone; “osteo” means bone. Skin surface cells are epithelial, so this malignant tumor is a carcinoma. Tumor names combine tissue and behavior: “oma” alone is usually benign, carcinoma is malignant epithelial tissue, and sarcoma is malignant connective tissue such as bone, fat or muscle.
questions.strategy: Read the ending first: plain “oma” is benign, “carcinoma” is epithelial, “sarcoma” is connective tissue. Then use the prefix to confirm the tissue.

questions.topic: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage
questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with lung cancer asks why a PET scan and more tests are needed before treatment starts. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage

options.text: “The scans confirm whether the tumor is cancer.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The biopsy already confirmed cancer. Further scans look for how far it has spread.

options.text: “The tests show how abnormal your cancer cells look.”
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem How abnormal the cells look is the grade, which comes from the biopsy sample, not from scans.

options.text: “The tests show how far it has spread, which guides treatment.”
options.rationale: Staging uses the TNM findings, tumor size, lymph nodes and distant spread, to describe the extent of disease. The stage guides which treatments will help.

options.text: “The tests are done so the team can plan your exact radiation dose.”
options.rationale: Correct but premature Radiation planning may come later, but the purpose of these tests is staging, which decides whether radiation is even used.

questions.takeaway: Staging (TNM: tumor, nodes, metastasis) describes how far the cancer has spread and guides treatment. Grade describes the cells and comes from the tissue sample.
questions.strategy: Ask what a scan can see: size and location. That is staging, not diagnosis (already done) or grade (needs a microscope).

questions.topic: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a community group about lowering cancer risk. Which statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

options.text: “Using a tanning bed twice a month is safe.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ultraviolet radiation from tanning beds is a physical carcinogen at any frequency.

options.text: “Quitting smoking is the biggest step I can take.”
options.rationale: Tobacco is linked to about 30% of cancers, the largest single preventable cause. Radon is a radioactive gas that seeps from soil and is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking. Limiting ultraviolet exposure reduces skin cancer risk.

options.text: “I will test my basement for radon gas.”
options.rationale: Tobacco is linked to about 30% of cancers, the largest single preventable cause. Radon is a radioactive gas that seeps from soil and is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking. Limiting ultraviolet exposure reduces skin cancer risk.

options.text: “Switching from cigarettes to cigars removes the risk.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cigars still expose the mouth, throat and lungs to tobacco carcinogens.

options.text: “I will wear sunscreen and avoid the midday sun.”
options.rationale: Tobacco is linked to about 30% of cancers, the largest single preventable cause. Radon is a radioactive gas that seeps from soil and is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking. Limiting ultraviolet exposure reduces skin cancer risk.

questions.takeaway: Primary prevention removes carcinogens: stop all tobacco, test for radon, and limit ultraviolet exposure from the sun and tanning beds.
questions.strategy: Each correct statement removes or limits a known carcinogen. Each wrong one only changes the form or amount of the same exposure.

questions.topic: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation
questions.stem: A 72 year old patient with no family history of cancer asks why colon cancer screening is still recommended. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

options.text: “Age itself is the strongest risk factor for most cancers.”
options.rationale: With age, DNA changes and exposures build up while immune defenses decline, so cancer risk rises even without a family history.

options.text: “Screening is only needed when cancer runs in families.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Most cancers occur in people with no family history. Average risk adults are screened too.

options.text: “After 70, screening is no longer useful for anyone.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Screening decisions after 75 are individualized, but at 72 screening is still recommended for a person in good health.

options.text: “Your risk is low, so screening is just a precaution.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept This understates the risk. Age is a major risk factor, so the patient's risk is not low.

questions.takeaway: Cancer risk rises with age because DNA damage accumulates and immune surveillance declines. Most cancers occur in people without a family history.
questions.strategy: The patient's age is the deciding cue. Reject options that make family history the only reason to screen.

questions.topic: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation
questions.stem: The nurse is taking a health history from a patient at a primary care visit. Select all of the findings that suggest an inherited cancer risk. Note: “Patient is 34 years old and walks 30 minutes daily. A parent was diagnosed with colon cancer at age 41. A grandparent had prostate cancer at age 84. A sibling and two cousins on the same side of the family had colon or uterine cancer. Patient quit smoking 5 years ago. A cousin was treated for a rare adrenal tumor. Patient drinks one glass of wine a week.”
questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

options.text: walks 30 minutes daily
options.rationale: Near miss concept Regular activity lowers risk and is not a genetic clue.

options.text: A parent was diagnosed with colon cancer at age 41
options.rationale: Cancer at an unusually young age is a key clue to an inherited syndrome. Several close relatives on one side with related cancers suggests an inherited pattern, such as Lynch syndrome. A rare cancer in the family is a clue to an inherited syndrome.

options.text: A grandparent had prostate cancer at age 84
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Prostate cancer at an advanced age is common and does not suggest an inherited pattern.

options.text: A sibling and two cousins on the same side of the family had colon or uterine cancer
options.rationale: Cancer at an unusually young age is a key clue to an inherited syndrome. Several close relatives on one side with related cancers suggests an inherited pattern, such as Lynch syndrome. A rare cancer in the family is a clue to an inherited syndrome.

options.text: quit smoking 5 years ago
options.rationale: Near miss concept Past smoking affects risk, but it is an exposure, not an inherited clue.

options.text: A cousin was treated for a rare adrenal tumor
options.rationale: Cancer at an unusually young age is a key clue to an inherited syndrome. Several close relatives on one side with related cancers suggests an inherited pattern, such as Lynch syndrome. A rare cancer in the family is a clue to an inherited syndrome.

questions.takeaway: Clues to inherited cancer risk are cancer at a young age, several close relatives with the same or related cancers, and rare cancers in the family. These prompt referral for genetic counseling.
questions.strategy: Separate inherited clues from lifestyle and from common, late cancers. Age at diagnosis and clustering on one side of the family are what count.

questions.topic: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation
questions.stem: A patient whose sibling has a BRCA2 mutation asks the nurse, “Should I get tested?” Which response is best?
questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

options.text: “Yes, you should get tested as soon as possible.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Advising testing without counseling skips the discussion of what results mean for the patient and family. The decision is the patient's after counseling.

options.text: “A genetic counselor can review the risks and benefits with you first.”
options.rationale: Genetic counseling belongs before and after testing. The nurse gives risk information and refers, and the patient decides.

options.text: “No, only people who already have cancer are tested.”
options.rationale: Absolute language People without cancer who have a family mutation are often offered testing. This statement is wrong.

options.text: “Your result will tell you for certain whether or not you will get cancer.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept A positive result shows higher risk, not certainty. This misstates what testing can tell.

questions.takeaway: The nurse provides risk information, not a diagnosis or a decision. A genetic counselor should be involved before and after testing.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that keeps the decision with the patient and brings in the right expert at the right time.

questions.topic: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation
questions.stem: After genetic counseling, a patient learns of a harmful BRCA1 gene change. Which statement indicates the patient understands the result?
questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

options.text: “My risk is higher, but I may never get cancer.”
options.rationale: A harmful gene change raises risk; it does not guarantee cancer. Screening and risk reduction options can lower the chance further.

options.text: “This means I already have cancer somewhere.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept A gene result is not a diagnosis. It describes inherited risk.

options.text: “My children will definitely inherit this change.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Each child has about a 50% chance of inheriting it, not a certainty.

options.text: “Since this is genetic, there is nothing at all that can lower my risk.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Closer screening, medicines and surgery can lower risk for gene carriers.

questions.takeaway: A harmful gene change means higher risk, not certain cancer. Options to lower risk include closer screening, medicines and preventive surgery.
questions.strategy: The correct statement holds two ideas at once: higher risk and not certain. Each wrong option turns risk into certainty or hopelessness.

questions.topic: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation
questions.stem: At a clinic visit, a patient mentions several changes. Which findings does the nurse recommend be evaluated for cancer? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

options.text: Muscle soreness for 3 days after starting a new workout
options.rationale: Near miss concept Soreness after new exercise has an obvious cause and resolves on its own.

options.text: Hoarseness that has lasted 6 weeks
options.rationale: A nagging cough or hoarseness is one of the seven warning signs of cancer. A sore that does not heal is a warning sign. An obvious change in a wart or mole is a warning sign of skin cancer.

options.text: A sore on the lip that has not healed in 5 weeks
options.rationale: A nagging cough or hoarseness is one of the seven warning signs of cancer. A sore that does not heal is a warning sign. An obvious change in a wart or mole is a warning sign of skin cancer.

options.text: A cough with a cold that started 4 days ago
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A short cough with a cold is expected; persistence is what makes it a warning sign.

options.text: A mole that has changed shape and color
options.rationale: A nagging cough or hoarseness is one of the seven warning signs of cancer. A sore that does not heal is a warning sign. An obvious change in a wart or mole is a warning sign of skin cancer.

questions.takeaway: The seven warning signs (CAUTION): change in bowel or bladder habits, a sore that does not heal, unusual bleeding or discharge, a thickening or lump, indigestion or trouble swallowing, an obvious change in a wart or mole, and a nagging cough or hoarseness.
questions.strategy: Two features make a finding a warning sign: it persists without an obvious cause, and it matches one of the CAUTION signs.

questions.topic: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation
questions.stem: A patient reports blood mixed in the stool for 3 weeks and asks for a home stool test kit. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Distinguish cancer risk reduction, screening, and diagnostic evaluation

options.text: “The kit is a good first step to look for hidden blood.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stool tests screen people without symptoms. Visible bleeding is already a symptom, so screening adds nothing.

options.text: “Repeat the test yearly if this one comes back normal.”
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Yearly stool testing is a screening plan. A normal result would not explain the bleeding the patient already has.

options.text: “The provider needs to see you for a diagnostic exam, such as a colonoscopy.”
options.rationale: Symptoms call for a diagnostic evaluation, not screening. A colonoscopy can find and biopsy the source.

options.text: “Bleeding like this is usually from hemorrhoids, so just watch it for another month or two.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Assuming a benign cause delays diagnosis. Rectal bleeding for 3 weeks needs evaluation.

questions.takeaway: Screening is for people without symptoms. A symptom such as rectal bleeding calls for a diagnostic evaluation.
questions.strategy: First ask: does the patient have a symptom? If yes, every screening option is the wrong tool.

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: A patient with breast cancer asks why the treatment plan differs from a friend's plan for the same cancer. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

options.text: “Plans depend on stage, tumor markers, your health and your goals.”
options.rationale: Treatment is chosen from the type and stage of cancer, tumor biomarkers, overall health and the patient's own goals, so two people with the same cancer can get different plans.

options.text: “Your provider prefers a different approach than your friend's.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Plans follow evidence based factors, not provider preference.

options.text: “The plan is based on the size of the tumor only.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Size is one part of staging, but nodes, spread, biomarkers, health and goals also matter.

options.text: “Your friend's cancer was probably more advanced than yours.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept This guesses about another patient and ignores the other factors in choosing treatment.

questions.takeaway: Treatment choice depends on the type and stage of cancer, tumor biomarkers, overall health and the patient's goals.
questions.strategy: Pick the global option that names all the factors; the others reduce treatment choice to one factor or to a guess.

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: A patient with cancer found in the liver, lungs and bones asks why surgery is not being offered. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

options.text: “Surgery is used only after chemotherapy has failed.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Surgery is often the first treatment for localized cancer. It is not reserved for after chemotherapy.

options.text: “Cancer in several organs needs treatment that reaches the whole body.”
options.rationale: Surgery and external beam radiation are local: they treat one site. Spread to several organs calls for systemic therapy, such as chemotherapy or immunotherapy, that travels through the blood.

options.text: “Surgery would remove the cancer but is too risky for you.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Even a safe surgery could not remove cancer in three organ systems. The reason is the spread, not the risk.

options.text: “Radiation to each organ works better than surgery.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Radiation is also local. Treating each site does not reach cells throughout the body.

questions.takeaway: Local treatments (surgery, external beam radiation) treat one site; systemic treatments (chemotherapy, immunotherapy, hormonal and targeted therapy) reach the whole body and are used for widespread cancer.
questions.strategy: Classify each option as local or systemic. Cancer in several organs needs systemic therapy.

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: The nurse reviews the surgical plans of six patients with cancer or cancer risk. For each plan, indicate the goal of the surgery.
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

rows.text: Bypassing a bowel blocked by widespread cancer to relieve vomiting
Removing the colon of a patient with familial adenomatous polyposis and no cancer yet
Removing an early lung tumor with clear margins and no spread
Removing as much of a large abdominal tumor as possible when it cannot all be removed
Removing a thyroid gland in a patient with an inherited RET gene change and no cancer
Removing a tissue sample from a new breast lump

questions.takeaway: Palliative surgery relieves symptoms and improves comfort without aiming to cure. Prophylactic surgery removes tissue at very high risk before cancer develops. Removing all of a localized tumor aims to cure. Debulking removes part of a tumor that cannot be fully removed so other treatments work better. A preventive removal in a person with a high risk gene change and no cancer is prophylactic. A biopsy obtains tissue to confirm whether a mass is cancer and what type. Prophylactic surgery prevents cancer in high risk tissue; diagnostic surgery gets tissue; curative surgery removes all localized cancer; debulking removes part of a tumor; palliative surgery relieves symptoms.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions for each plan: is there cancer yet, and is the aim to prevent, confirm, cure, reduce or relieve?

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: A patient asks why radiation is scheduled 5 days a week for 6 weeks instead of one large dose. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

options.text: “Small daily doses let normal tissue recover between treatments.”
options.rationale: Dividing the dose, called fractionation, kills more cancer cells over time while normal tissue repairs between sessions, so side effects are fewer.

options.text: “One large dose would make you radioactive afterward.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept External beam radiation never makes the patient radioactive, whatever the dose.

options.text: “The machine can only deliver a small dose each day.”
options.rationale: Absolute language The schedule is set by biology, not by machine limits.

options.text: “Daily treatment gives your cancer less time to spread.”
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem The daily schedule exists to protect normal tissue, not to outpace spread.

questions.takeaway: Radiation is fractionated into small daily doses so cancer cells are killed while normal tissue recovers between treatments.
questions.strategy: The reason must explain why small doses beat one large dose: the protection of normal tissue.

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: The nurse is assigned four patients receiving cancer treatment. Which patient requires radiation safety precautions?
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

options.text: A patient receiving external beam radiation to the chest
options.rationale: Near miss concept External beam radiation comes from a machine outside the body, so the patient never gives off radiation.

options.text: A patient who finished IV chemotherapy 6 hours ago
options.rationale: Near miss concept This patient needs hazardous drug precautions for body fluids, not radiation precautions.

options.text: A patient with a sealed radioactive implant in place
options.rationale: Brachytherapy places the source inside the body, so the patient emits radiation while it is in place. Time, distance and shielding apply.

options.text: A patient who had a CT scan with contrast today
options.rationale: Near miss concept A CT scan uses x rays only during the scan, and contrast is not radioactive.

questions.takeaway: Only internal radiation (brachytherapy) makes the patient a radiation source. External beam radiation does not; chemotherapy needs hazardous drug precautions instead.
questions.strategy: Ask where the radiation source is. Only a source inside the body requires radiation precautions; watch for the chemotherapy patient, who needs a different kind of precaution.

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: A patient starting immunotherapy asks why the nurse expects less hair loss than with the chemotherapy a relative received. Which explanation is accurate?
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

options.text: “Immunotherapy helps your immune system attack the cancer cells.”
options.rationale: Chemotherapy kills all fast dividing cells, including hair follicles. Immunotherapy works by helping the immune system find and attack cancer, so hair loss is uncommon.

options.text: “Immunotherapy is a weaker form of chemotherapy.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Immunotherapy is a different class of treatment, not a weaker chemotherapy.

options.text: “Immunotherapy is given at a much lower dose.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dose is not the reason. The mechanism of action differs.

options.text: “Immunotherapy only kills the fast dividing cells in tumors.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Killing fast dividing cells describes chemotherapy, which cannot tell tumor cells from hair follicles.

questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy kills fast dividing cells, healthy or not; immunotherapy helps the immune system attack cancer. Side effects follow the mechanism.
questions.strategy: Explain side effects through mechanism. Hair loss comes from killing dividing cells, which immunotherapy does not do.

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy every 21 days asks, “Why can't I get it every week to finish sooner?” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

options.text: “Weekly doses would not reach the tumor.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Every dose reaches the tumor through the blood. The gap is about healthy cells.

options.text: “The rest period lets your healthy cells recover.”
options.rationale: Chemotherapy is given in cycles so the bone marrow and other healthy tissues can recover before the next dose.

options.text: “The cancer needs time to grow so the drug works better.”
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Cycles are not timed to let the cancer grow; they are timed for normal tissue recovery.

options.text: “Your body needs time to clear the drug from your blood.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Most drugs clear within days. The 21 days are for blood counts to recover from the nadir.

questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy is given in cycles so healthy cells, especially the bone marrow, can recover between doses.
questions.strategy: The schedule protects normal tissue. Choose the option about healthy cells, not about the drug or the tumor.

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: A patient's breast tumor tested positive for HER2. The patient asks why that test mattered before starting trastuzumab. Which response is accurate?
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

options.text: “The drug only works when the tumor has that target.”
options.rationale: Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody, a targeted therapy that attaches to the HER2 protein. Without the target, it has nothing to act on.

options.text: “The test shows how much of the chemotherapy your body can handle.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tolerance is judged by health and blood counts, not by HER2 status.

options.text: “A positive test means the cancer has spread.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept HER2 is a tumor marker, not a measure of spread. Staging shows spread.

options.text: “The test decides how many cycles you will need.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The number of cycles comes from the treatment plan, not from the target test.

questions.takeaway: Targeted therapies and monoclonal antibodies attach to or block a specific target the cancer has, so the tumor is tested for that target first.
questions.strategy: Connect the drug to its target. A targeted drug needs the target, which is why biomarker testing comes first.

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give a patient's first dose of IV chemotherapy. Which information does the nurse verify before the dose is prepared?
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

options.text: The patient's current height and weight
options.rationale: Many chemotherapy doses are based on body surface area, which is calculated from height and weight. An outdated weight gives a wrong dose.

options.text: The patient's blood type and Rh factor
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blood type is needed for transfusion, not for chemotherapy dosing.

options.text: The patient's preferred pain medicine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pain control matters, but it does not affect the chemotherapy dose.

options.text: The patient's most recent chest x ray
options.rationale: Near miss concept A chest x ray is not used to calculate chemotherapy doses.

questions.takeaway: Many chemotherapy doses are calculated from body surface area, so a current, measured height and weight are verified before preparation.
questions.strategy: Ask what the dose depends on. Body surface area comes from height and weight.

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: A patient with leukemia that has spread to the cerebrospinal fluid will receive intrathecal methotrexate. The patient asks why it is not given IV. Which response is accurate?
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

options.text: “IV drugs work too fast to be safe for you.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Speed is not the reason. The issue is whether the drug reaches the cerebrospinal fluid.

options.text: “Intrathecal dosing avoids all side effects.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Intrathecal chemotherapy still has side effects, such as headache and infection risk at the site.

options.text: “Most IV drugs do not reach the fluid around your brain.”
options.rationale: The blood brain barrier keeps most IV drugs out of the cerebrospinal fluid. Intrathecal dosing delivers the drug directly into it.

options.text: “Intrathecal dosing is used when your veins are too fragile for any IV.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Fragile veins call for a central line, not an intrathecal route.

questions.takeaway: Intrathecal chemotherapy is given into the cerebrospinal fluid because the blood brain barrier blocks most IV drugs from reaching it.
questions.strategy: Name the route, then ask what problem it solves: getting the drug past the blood brain barrier.

questions.topic: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions
questions.stem: Three weeks into radiation to the head and neck, a patient reports a sore, dry mouth and trouble swallowing. Which actions does the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

options.text: Rinse often with a salt and baking soda solution
options.rationale: Bland rinses clean the mouth and soothe mucositis without irritating it. Soft, moist foods are easier to swallow and less painful on inflamed tissue. Frequent sips relieve dry mouth from salivary gland damage. Painful swallowing reduces intake, so weight is tracked to catch malnutrition early.

options.text: Use an alcohol based mouthwash after meals
options.rationale: Near miss concept Alcohol dries and burns inflamed tissue, making mucositis worse.

options.text: Offer soft, moist foods such as yogurt and mashed potatoes
options.rationale: Bland rinses clean the mouth and soothe mucositis without irritating it. Soft, moist foods are easier to swallow and less painful on inflamed tissue. Frequent sips relieve dry mouth from salivary gland damage. Painful swallowing reduces intake, so weight is tracked to catch malnutrition early.

options.text: Sip water often throughout the day
options.rationale: Bland rinses clean the mouth and soothe mucositis without irritating it. Soft, moist foods are easier to swallow and less painful on inflamed tissue. Frequent sips relieve dry mouth from salivary gland damage. Painful swallowing reduces intake, so weight is tracked to catch malnutrition early.

options.text: Use lemon glycerin swabs to moisten the lips and mouth
options.rationale: Near miss concept Lemon glycerin swabs dry and irritate the mouth and are avoided in mucositis.

options.text: Weigh the patient at each visit
options.rationale: Bland rinses clean the mouth and soothe mucositis without irritating it. Soft, moist foods are easier to swallow and less painful on inflamed tissue. Frequent sips relieve dry mouth from salivary gland damage. Painful swallowing reduces intake, so weight is tracked to catch malnutrition early.

questions.takeaway: Head and neck radiation causes mucositis, dry mouth and trouble swallowing. Use bland rinses, frequent sips, soft moist foods and weight checks; avoid alcohol rinses and lemon glycerin.
questions.strategy: Every correct action soothes the mouth, moistens it, eases swallowing or watches nutrition. The wrong ones dry or irritate inflamed tissue.

questions.topic: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions
questions.stem: Nurses on different shifts describe a patient's chemotherapy diarrhea as “bad,” “moderate” and “a lot.” Which action best makes the documentation consistent?
questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

options.text: Grade the diarrhea with the CTCAE scale each shift
options.rationale: The Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grade side effects from 1 to 5 using defined criteria, so every nurse describes the same severity the same way.

options.text: Ask the patient to rate the diarrhea from 0 to 10
options.rationale: Near miss concept A 0 to 10 rating is subjective and is not the standard tool for grading treatment side effects.

options.text: Write a detailed narrative note on each shift
options.rationale: Near miss concept Narratives still vary between nurses. A standardized scale is what removes the inconsistency.

options.text: Record only the number of stools each day
options.rationale: Absolute language Stool count is part of grading, but alone it misses other criteria such as the effect on daily activities.

questions.takeaway: The CTCAE is a standardized scale for grading and documenting treatment side effects, so changes can be compared over time and between nurses.
questions.strategy: The problem is inconsistent wording, so the fix is a shared scale.

questions.topic: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions
questions.stem: Before the third chemotherapy cycle, a patient begins vomiting in the parking lot on seeing the clinic. Which intervention best addresses this problem?
questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

options.text: Give the prescribed antiemetic only after chemotherapy starts
options.rationale: Absolute language This is anticipatory nausea, which starts before treatment. Waiting until chemotherapy starts misses it.

options.text: Delay the cycle until the vomiting stops on its own
options.rationale: Near miss concept Delaying treatment does not treat a learned response and can harm the cancer plan.

options.text: Teach guided imagery and relaxation to use before visits
options.rationale: Anticipatory nausea is a conditioned response. Relaxation, guided imagery and distraction, along with prescribed antianxiety medicine before visits, help prevent it.

options.text: Encourage a large meal before each appointment
options.rationale: Near miss concept A large meal tends to worsen nausea. Small, bland meals are preferred.

questions.takeaway: Anticipatory nausea is triggered by cues linked to past treatment. Prevent it with relaxation, guided imagery, distraction and prescribed antianxiety medicine before treatment, and by controlling nausea well in every cycle.
questions.strategy: Name the type from the timing: before treatment, triggered by a cue. Then choose the intervention that targets a learned response.

questions.topic: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions
questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for highly emetogenic chemotherapy at 1000. Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions
questions.sentence: The nurse gives the prescribed ondansetron [[1]] because antiemetics work best when [[2]].

options.text: at the first sign of nausea
after the infusion is complete
only if the patient vomits twice
at 0930, before the infusion starts
the stomach is completely empty
combined with a full liquid diet
given to prevent symptoms rather than treat them
given in the largest possible dose

questions.takeaway: Antiemetics are given 30 to 60 minutes before chemotherapy so they are working when the drug arrives. Prevention is the goal in chemotherapy induced nausea and vomiting; scheduled dosing keeps blood levels steady. Antiemetics for chemotherapy are given before treatment begins and on schedule afterward, to prevent nausea and vomiting rather than chase it.
questions.strategy: Prevention beats rescue: the drug must be in the body before the chemotherapy is.

questions.topic: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions
questions.stem: Four patients receiving chemotherapy call the clinic. Which patient does the nurse call back first?
questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

options.text: A 45 year old patient with nausea who is keeping down fluids and soup
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nausea with adequate fluid intake can be managed with the antiemetic plan.

options.text: A 60 year old patient with hair loss who feels embarrassed
options.rationale: Near miss concept Body image distress is real and is addressed, but it is not physiologically urgent.

options.text: A 52 year old patient with a metallic taste in the mouth
options.rationale: Near miss concept Taste changes affect appetite but are not urgent.

options.text: An 84 year old patient who vomited 6 times overnight and is dizzy
options.rationale: Older adults have less body water reserve and become dehydrated quickly. Repeated vomiting with dizziness suggests dehydration that needs prompt treatment.

questions.takeaway: Persistent chemotherapy induced vomiting is especially dangerous in older adults, who dehydrate faster and are prone to falls and kidney injury.
questions.strategy: Age matters here because it changes how fast fluid loss becomes dangerous. Combine the vomiting with the dizziness and the age.

questions.topic: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions
questions.stem: A patient is receiving a short IV push of fluorouracil, a drug known to cause mouth sores. Which action during the infusion helps prevent mucositis?
questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

options.text: Rinse the mouth with hydrogen peroxide
options.rationale: Near miss concept Peroxide damages healing tissue and is not used to prevent mucositis.

options.text: Have the patient hold ice chips in the mouth
options.rationale: Ice chips during the infusion constrict mouth blood vessels so less drug reaches the lining. This oral cryotherapy is used with selected drugs such as fluorouracil.

options.text: Have the patient drink hot tea to stay warm
options.rationale: Near miss concept Warmth increases blood flow to the mouth, which is the opposite of the goal.

options.text: Brush the teeth firmly during the infusion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Firm brushing injures the lining. A soft brush is used gently between treatments.

questions.takeaway: Ice chips during selected chemotherapy infusions, such as fluorouracil, help prevent mucositis by limiting blood flow to the mouth. Cold is avoided with oxaliplatin, which causes cold sensitivity.
questions.strategy: Think about the mechanism: less blood flow to the mouth means less drug in the lining.

questions.topic: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions
questions.stem: A patient who finished chemotherapy last week asks about the hair that fell out. Which statement indicates understanding?
questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

options.text: “My hair may start growing back in about a month.”
options.rationale: Regrowth often begins about 3 to 4 weeks after chemotherapy ends, and the new hair may differ in color or texture.

options.text: “My hair will grow back exactly the same color and texture as it was before.”
options.rationale: Absolute language New hair can be a different color or texture, so “exactly” is not accurate.

options.text: “My hair loss from chemotherapy is permanent.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Chemotherapy hair loss is usually temporary.

options.text: “I can skip covering my scalp outdoors.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The bare scalp burns easily, so a hat or sunscreen is needed outdoors.

questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy hair loss is usually temporary; regrowth may begin about a month after treatment ends, sometimes with a new color or texture. Protect the scalp from sun and cold.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that gets both the timing and the uncertainty right, and reject absolutes.

questions.topic: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions
questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has missed two doses of an oral medicine because of trouble remembering. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

options.text: Tell the patient to double the next dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept Doubling a missed dose is unsafe and not part of managing memory changes.

options.text: Provide a written medicine schedule
options.rationale: Written instructions give the patient something to check later, which is the most helpful step for chemotherapy related memory changes. Reminders reduce reliance on memory.

options.text: Suggest stopping chemotherapy until memory improves
options.rationale: Correct but premature Memory changes are managed with supports; stopping treatment is the provider's decision and not the first step.

options.text: Set phone alarms for each dose time
options.rationale: Written instructions give the patient something to check later, which is the most helpful step for chemotherapy related memory changes. Reminders reduce reliance on memory.

options.text: Advise avoiding books and puzzles to rest the brain
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mental activity is encouraged; avoiding it does not help.

questions.takeaway: For chemotherapy related memory changes, use written instructions, reminders and routines so the patient does not depend on memory alone.
questions.strategy: Each correct action supports memory from outside the brain. Each wrong action is unsafe or unhelpful.

questions.topic: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions
questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL and reports being exhausted after showering. Which intervention does the nurse include?
questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

options.text: Encourage a full bath and shampoo every morning
options.rationale: Absolute language A full routine at once uses more energy than the patient has. Activities are spaced out instead.

options.text: Plan rest periods between daily activities
options.rationale: Anemia lowers oxygen delivery, so energy is limited. Spacing activities with rest periods conserves energy.

options.text: Teach use of an electric razor and soft toothbrush
options.rationale: Near miss concept These protect against bleeding from low platelets, not fatigue from anemia.

options.text: Have the patient avoid crowds and sick contacts
options.rationale: Near miss concept This protects against infection from neutropenia, not fatigue from anemia.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the low cell: anemia means fatigue, so conserve energy; low platelets means bleeding precautions; neutropenia means infection precautions.
questions.strategy: Name the low cell first, then pick the intervention for that cell. Two distractors are correct for a different cell.

questions.topic: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment
questions.stem: A nurse floated from a medical unit without chemotherapy training is assigned a patient due for IV chemotherapy. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.objective: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment

options.text: Give it after reviewing the drug guide carefully
options.rationale: Near miss concept Reviewing a drug guide does not replace specialized training and demonstrated competency.

options.text: Have another nurse watch while the dose is given
options.rationale: Near miss concept Supervision by any nurse does not make the floated nurse qualified to give chemotherapy.

options.text: Ask the charge nurse for a chemotherapy trained nurse
options.rationale: Only RNs who have completed specialized training and shown competency may give chemotherapy. The floated nurse can still provide the rest of the care.

options.text: Delay the dose until the next shift
options.rationale: Near miss concept Delaying treatment is unnecessary when a qualified nurse can give it now.

questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy is given only by RNs who completed specialized training and showed competency. An untrained nurse gets a qualified nurse to give it.
questions.strategy: This is about scope, not knowledge: training plus demonstrated competency is required.

questions.topic: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a caregiver of a patient who received IV chemotherapy today and is going home. Which instructions does the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment

options.text: Wear gloves when handling vomit, urine or stool
options.rationale: Chemotherapy is excreted in body fluids for about 48 hours, so gloves protect the caregiver. Double flushing with the lid down limits splashing of drug in the urine and stool. Separate washing keeps drug residue off the household's other clothes. Hand hygiene removes any drug that reached the skin. Sealing contaminated items keeps the drug contained.

options.text: Flush the toilet twice with the lid closed
options.rationale: Chemotherapy is excreted in body fluids for about 48 hours, so gloves protect the caregiver. Double flushing with the lid down limits splashing of drug in the urine and stool. Separate washing keeps drug residue off the household's other clothes. Hand hygiene removes any drug that reached the skin. Sealing contaminated items keeps the drug contained.

options.text: Wash soiled linens separately from other laundry
options.rationale: Chemotherapy is excreted in body fluids for about 48 hours, so gloves protect the caregiver. Double flushing with the lid down limits splashing of drug in the urine and stool. Separate washing keeps drug residue off the household's other clothes. Hand hygiene removes any drug that reached the skin. Sealing contaminated items keeps the drug contained.

options.text: Wash hands with soap and water after removing gloves
options.rationale: Chemotherapy is excreted in body fluids for about 48 hours, so gloves protect the caregiver. Double flushing with the lid down limits splashing of drug in the urine and stool. Separate washing keeps drug residue off the household's other clothes. Hand hygiene removes any drug that reached the skin. Sealing contaminated items keeps the drug contained.

options.text: Share the toilet without any precautions after 2 hours
options.rationale: Absolute language Drug stays in body fluids for about 48 hours, not 2 hours.

options.text: Place soiled pads in a sealed plastic bag before discarding
options.rationale: Chemotherapy is excreted in body fluids for about 48 hours, so gloves protect the caregiver. Double flushing with the lid down limits splashing of drug in the urine and stool. Separate washing keeps drug residue off the household's other clothes. Hand hygiene removes any drug that reached the skin. Sealing contaminated items keeps the drug contained.

questions.takeaway: For about 48 hours after chemotherapy, body fluids contain the drug: wear gloves, flush twice with the lid closed, wash linens separately, bag soiled items and wash hands.
questions.strategy: Every correct instruction contains the drug in body fluids. The one wrong instruction gets the time frame wrong.

questions.topic: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a caregiver about the patient's oral capecitabine tablets. Which caregiver statement requires further teaching?
questions.objective: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment

options.text: “I will wear gloves if I need to touch the tablets.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Gloves protect the caregiver, because oral chemotherapy is hazardous too.

options.text: “I will crush the tablets in applesauce if they are hard to swallow.”
options.rationale: Crushing hazardous tablets releases drug dust and can change the dose. If swallowing is a problem, the nurse contacts the pharmacist or provider about another form.

options.text: “I will store the tablets in their own container away from other family medicines.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Separate storage prevents mix ups and exposure.

options.text: “I will wash my hands after giving the dose.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hand hygiene after handling is correct.

questions.takeaway: Oral chemotherapy is hazardous: handle it with gloves, store it separately, and never crush or split it. Swallowing problems go to the pharmacist or provider.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that exposes someone to the drug or changes the dose.

questions.topic: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment
questions.stem: A patient has a sealed radioactive implant in place. The nurse observes visitors and staff in the room. For each action, indicate whether it is appropriate or requires the nurse to intervene.
questions.objective: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment

rows.text: A nursing assistant picks up a dislodged implant with gloved hands
A staff member wears a radiation dosimeter badge
A visitor plans to stay for the whole afternoon
A visitor brings a 10 year old child to the bedside
A visitor sits in a chair 6 feet from the bed
The nurse clusters care to limit time in the room

questions.takeaway: A dislodged source is never handled with hands. It is picked up with long forceps and placed in the lead container. The badge tracks each person's cumulative exposure. Visits are limited in length, often to 30 minutes a day, to limit time near the source. Children are not allowed to visit while the implant is in place because they are more sensitive to radiation. Distance lowers exposure; visitors stay at least 6 feet away. Less time near the source means less exposure. Time, distance and shielding: limit time, keep distance, use shielding, badge every staff member, keep children away, and pick up a dislodged source only with long forceps into the lead container.
questions.strategy: Test each action against time, distance and shielding. Anything that adds time, removes distance or handles the source directly requires intervention.

questions.topic: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response
questions.stem: The nurse reviews the note for a patient with neutropenia after chemotherapy. Select all of the findings that suggest the infection is progressing to sepsis. Note: “Day 10 after chemotherapy. Temperature 38.4 °C. Blood pressure 86/50 mm Hg, down from 118/72 mm Hg this morning. Newly confused about the date. Hair thinning on the scalp. Urine output 60 mL over the last 4 hours. Reports mild nausea after lunch. Skin is warm.”
questions.objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response

options.text: Temperature 38.4 °C
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fever signals infection, which is already known. It does not by itself show progression to sepsis.

options.text: Blood pressure 86/50 mm Hg, down from 118/72 mm Hg this morning
options.rationale: Falling blood pressure shows poor perfusion, a sign of sepsis. New confusion signals reduced brain perfusion in sepsis. Output of 15 mL/hr is below 30 mL/hr and shows poor kidney perfusion.

options.text: Newly confused about the date
options.rationale: Falling blood pressure shows poor perfusion, a sign of sepsis. New confusion signals reduced brain perfusion in sepsis. Output of 15 mL/hr is below 30 mL/hr and shows poor kidney perfusion.

options.text: Hair thinning on the scalp
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Hair loss is an expected chemotherapy effect.

options.text: Urine output 60 mL over the last 4 hours
options.rationale: Falling blood pressure shows poor perfusion, a sign of sepsis. New confusion signals reduced brain perfusion in sepsis. Output of 15 mL/hr is below 30 mL/hr and shows poor kidney perfusion.

options.text: Reports mild nausea after lunch
options.rationale: Near miss concept Mild nausea is a common chemotherapy effect.

questions.takeaway: In a neutropenic patient with infection, hypotension, new confusion and low urine output signal progression to sepsis. Sepsis can progress fast in neutropenia.
questions.strategy: Fever only says there is an infection. Sepsis shows up as organ perfusion failing: pressure, mind and kidneys.

questions.topic: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response
questions.stem: A patient with leukemia has blood oozing from the IV site, gums and nose and new blood in the urine. Which explanation is most likely?
questions.objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response

options.text: Clotting factors are being used up by widespread clotting
options.rationale: In disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), clotting is triggered throughout the body, using up platelets and clotting factors, so the patient bleeds from many sites at once.

options.text: The IV catheter has punctured through the vein
options.rationale: Near miss concept A misplaced catheter explains bleeding at one site, not the gums, nose and urine.

options.text: The patient is brushing the teeth too firmly
options.rationale: Near miss concept Firm brushing could explain gum bleeding but not bleeding from the nose, urine and IV site.

options.text: High white cell counts are blocking the blood vessels
options.rationale: Near miss concept Leukostasis causes clogging problems, not oozing from many sites.

questions.takeaway: Bleeding from multiple sites at once in a patient with cancer suggests DIC, in which widespread clotting consumes platelets and clotting factors.
questions.strategy: Count the sites. A single cause at one site cannot explain bleeding everywhere at once.

questions.topic: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response
questions.stem: A patient with breast cancer that has spread to bone reports new constipation, increased thirst and feeling tired. Which laboratory result does the nurse check first?
questions.objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response

options.text: Serum calcium
options.rationale: Bone metastases release calcium. Constipation, thirst and fatigue are early, subtle signs of hypercalcemia.

options.text: Serum sodium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Low sodium causes confusion and headache, not constipation and thirst together.

options.text: Platelet count
options.rationale: Near miss concept Platelets relate to bleeding risk, which these findings do not suggest.

options.text: Serum potassium
options.rationale: Near miss concept Potassium changes cause muscle and heart rhythm problems, not this pattern.

questions.takeaway: Constipation, thirst and fatigue in a patient with bone metastases are early signs of hypercalcemia; check the calcium before it progresses to confusion and dysrhythmias.
questions.strategy: Link the history to the lab: bone metastases release calcium. Then check that the symptoms fit high calcium.

questions.topic: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response
questions.stem: A patient with lung cancer reports that shirt collars feel tight. The face and neck are swollen, neck veins are distended, and the patient now has a high pitched sound with each breath. Complete the bow tie.
questions.objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response

options.text: Encourage a large glass of water
Place the patient flat with legs raised
Raise the head of the bed
Start an IV in the right arm
Call the rapid response team
Spinal cord compression
Hypercalcemia
Tumor lysis syndrome
Superior vena cava syndrome
Urine specific gravity
Oxygen saturation
Bowel sounds
Deep tendon reflexes
Airway sounds and respiratory effort

questions.takeaway: Elevation lets blood drain from the head and eases breathing. Stridor means the airway is narrowing, which is an emergency. A lung tumor compressing the superior vena cava blocks blood return from the head, neck and arms. Saturation shows whether swelling is affecting gas exchange. Stridor can progress to airway obstruction. Superior vena cava syndrome causes swelling of the face, neck and arms with distended neck veins. Stridor signals airway narrowing: raise the head of the bed, get help and watch the airway.
questions.strategy: Swelling above the heart with distended neck veins points to a blocked superior vena cava. Stridor makes the airway the priority.

questions.topic: Plan patient and caregiver teaching for symptom management, follow up, and survivorship
questions.stem: A patient treated with doxorubicin and chest radiation 4 years ago comes for a survivorship visit. Which report requires follow up?
questions.objective: Plan patient and caregiver teaching for symptom management, follow up, and survivorship

options.text: Hair has grown back thinner than before
options.rationale: Near miss concept Changes in hair texture are common after chemotherapy and are not dangerous.

options.text: Short of breath when climbing one flight of stairs
options.rationale: Doxorubicin can damage the heart and chest radiation can cause lung fibrosis years later. New exertional shortness of breath needs evaluation.

options.text: Feels anxious before each yearly scan
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Scan anxiety is common and is addressed, but it is not a sign of a late physical effect.

options.text: A scar that is lighter than the nearby skin
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A pale, healed scar is expected.

questions.takeaway: Late effects of cancer treatment include heart and lung damage, fibrosis in a radiation field, neuropathy, fertility changes and second cancers. Survivors are monitored for years.
questions.strategy: Link the past treatment to the organ it can damage: doxorubicin harms the heart and chest radiation the lungs.

questions.topic: Plan patient and caregiver teaching for symptom management, follow up, and survivorship
questions.stem: After breast cancer surgery with axillary lymph node removal, which patient statement requires further teaching?
questions.objective: Plan patient and caregiver teaching for symptom management, follow up, and survivorship

options.text: “I will wear gloves when I work in the garden.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Protecting the arm from cuts lowers the risk of infection and lymphedema.

options.text: “I will report any new swelling or feeling of heaviness in that arm.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Early report of swelling lets lymphedema be treated sooner.

options.text: “I will use my electric razor for my underarm.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept An electric razor reduces nicks on the affected side.

options.text: “I will carry heavy grocery bags with that arm right away.”
options.rationale: Heavy lifting soon after surgery strains the arm and can trigger lymphedema. Activity is increased gradually as advised.

questions.takeaway: After axillary node removal, protect the arm from injury, report new swelling or heaviness, and increase lifting gradually to lower the risk of lymphedema.
questions.strategy: This asks for the wrong statement. Find the one that overloads or injures the arm.

questions.topic: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment
questions.stem: A patient with lung cancer that has spread to the spine starts radiation to relieve back pain. Which statement indicates understanding of the treatment goal?
questions.objective: Compare the goals and common types of cancer treatment

options.text: “This radiation should cure my cancer.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Radiation to one site cannot cure cancer that has already spread. The goal here is comfort.

options.text: “After this, I can stop my pain medicine.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Radiation takes days to weeks to ease pain, so pain medicine continues.

options.text: “The goal is to shrink the tumor so my back hurts less.”
options.rationale: This is palliative radiation: it shrinks the tumor pressing on the spine to relieve pain and improve quality of life.

options.text: “Radiation to my spine will stop the cancer from spreading any further in my body.”
options.rationale: Absolute language Radiation to one site does not stop spread elsewhere in the body.

questions.takeaway: Treatment aimed at symptoms in spread cancer is palliative: it relieves pain or pressure but does not cure.
questions.strategy: Name the goal first. Spread cancer plus a symptom target means palliative.

questions.topic: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response
questions.stem: Twenty hours after the first chemotherapy dose for a large lymphoma, a patient has potassium 6.4 mEq/L, phosphate 6.8 mg/dL, uric acid 11 mg/dL and urine output 20 mL/hr. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response

options.text: Give the scheduled oral allopurinol dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept Allopurinol lowers future uric acid production but does nothing for the potassium that threatens the heart now.

options.text: Place on a cardiac monitor and notify the provider
options.rationale: These results are tumor lysis syndrome. A potassium of 6.4 mEq/L can cause fatal dysrhythmias, so the heart is monitored and the provider is called now.

options.text: Restrict potassium rich foods on the meal tray
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diet changes are far too slow for a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L.

options.text: Encourage the patient to drink more water throughout the next few hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hydration matters, but low urine output and high potassium need urgent provider orders, not oral fluids alone.

questions.takeaway: Tumor lysis syndrome raises potassium, phosphate and uric acid and lowers calcium. The most immediate threat is hyperkalemia to the heart, then the kidneys.
questions.strategy: Several options help tumor lysis, but only one addresses the finding that can kill first: the potassium.

questions.topic: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response
questions.stem: The oncology nurse reviews six patients with new findings. For each finding, indicate the oncologic emergency it most suggests.
questions.objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response

rows.text: Back pain that is worse lying down and new trouble starting urination
Facial swelling that is worse in the morning and a tight shirt collar
Weight gain of 2 kg, confusion and sodium 121 mEq/L
Numb lips and muscle cramps the day after a first chemotherapy dose
Constipation, thirst and fatigue in a patient with bone metastases
New leg weakness with numbness below the waist

questions.takeaway: Back pain worse lying flat, then bladder changes, signals pressure on the cord. Blocked return of blood from the head causes swelling, worse after lying flat overnight. Retained water dilutes sodium, causing weight gain and confusion. Phosphate released from dying cells binds calcium, so calcium falls, causing numbness and cramps. Bone breakdown releases calcium; constipation, thirst and fatigue are early signs. Motor and sensory loss below a level means the cord is compressed; this is an emergency. Match the emergency by its signature: back pain worse lying down (cord compression), facial swelling (superior vena cava), low sodium with water gain (SIADH), low calcium signs after chemotherapy (tumor lysis), constipation and thirst with bone metastases (hypercalcemia).
questions.strategy: Find the one cue in each row that only one emergency explains, then confirm with the setting.

questions.topic: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment
questions.stem: While hanging IV chemotherapy, the nurse knocks over the bag and about 100 mL spills on the floor. No one has been splashed. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.objective: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment

options.text: Restrict the area and put on spill kit protection
options.rationale: The first step is to keep others away and protect yourself: double gloves, gown, eye protection and a respirator from the spill kit. Then contain and clean the spill.

options.text: Wipe the spill with paper towels and discard them
options.rationale: Near miss concept Wiping without protection exposes the nurse, and regular trash is not used for hazardous waste.

options.text: Call housekeeping to mop the floor
options.rationale: Near miss concept Chemotherapy spills are cleaned by trained staff with a spill kit, not routine mopping.

options.text: Notify the provider that the dose was lost
options.rationale: Near miss concept The provider is told so the dose can be replaced, but the hazard is controlled first.

questions.takeaway: For a chemotherapy spill, secure the area, put on the protective equipment from the spill kit, contain and clean the spill, and dispose of it as hazardous waste; then report it.
questions.strategy: Safety first for everyone near the spill, then cleanup, then reporting.

questions.topic: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions
questions.stem: On day 9 after chemotherapy, a patient's platelets are 18,000/mm3 and the patient is constipated. Which prescription does the nurse question?
questions.objective: Identify common treatment side effects and appropriate nursing interventions

options.text: Oral docusate twice daily
options.rationale: Near miss concept A stool softener prevents straining, which lowers bleeding risk.

options.text: Acetaminophen for a headache
options.rationale: Near miss concept Acetaminophen does not affect platelet function, so it is preferred over aspirin and NSAIDs.

options.text: Bisacodyl rectal suppository
options.rationale: With platelets below 20,000/mm3, anything inserted into the rectum can tear the lining and cause bleeding. Rectal suppositories, enemas and rectal temperatures are avoided.

options.text: A soft toothbrush for oral care
options.rationale: Near miss concept A soft brush protects the gums when platelets are low.

questions.takeaway: At the nadir with very low platelets, avoid rectal routes, injections when possible, aspirin and NSAIDs, and anything that injures mucosa; use stool softeners and soft toothbrushes.
questions.strategy: Read the platelet count, then look for the option that injures a mucous membrane.

questions.stem: Which statement by a patient receiving external beam radiation indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will wash the marks off at the end of each week so the skin can recover."
options.rationale: The skin markings locate the treatment field and must not be removed. The other three statements are all correct teaching: loose cotton clothing, mild soap with no unprescribed products on the field, and lifelong sun protection of the treated area.

options.text: "I will wear loose cotton clothing over the treated area."
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Correct. Friction and heat are what break that skin down.

options.text: "I will protect that area from the sun for the rest of my life."
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Correct, and it really is for life. That skin never fully recovers.

options.text: "I will use only the mild soap and nothing else on that skin unless it is prescribed."
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Correct. Mild soap only, and nothing else goes on it.

questions.takeaway: Do not remove the markings. Everything else about radiation skin care is about gentleness.
questions.strategy: On a need for further teaching item, you are hunting the one wrong statement among three correct ones.

questions.stem: A patient with a large lymphoma burden is 24 hours into chemotherapy. Potassium is 6.0, phosphate is elevated, calcium is 7.2 and creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.8. What should the nurse recognize and anticipate?

options.text: Hyperparathyroidism from bone metastases; expect bisphosphonates
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would raise calcium, not lower it.

options.text: Expected post chemotherapy lab changes that need no intervention
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Normalizes a life threatening emergency.

options.text: Acute kidney injury from the chemotherapy drug alone; hold the dose
options.rationale: Near miss concept Explains the creatinine and not the potassium, phosphate and calcium pattern.

options.text: Tumor lysis syndrome; expect IV fluids, monitoring and potassium lowering
options.rationale: The pattern is the diagnosis: cells dying in bulk dump potassium, phosphate and uric acid, the phosphate binds calcium so the calcium falls, and the uric acid and phosphate injure the kidneys, which is the rising creatinine. High tumor burden plus the first day or two of treatment is the setting. Fluids and monitoring come first, and the potassium is the thing that kills in the next hour.

questions.takeaway: Potassium up, phosphate up, calcium down, creatinine up, within 48 hours of treatment. That is the whole syndrome.
questions.strategy: Four values moving in a specific pattern is a syndrome question, not four separate problems.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic prostate cancer reports new severe back pain that is worse when lying down, and today says his legs feel heavy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Escalate immediately, because this pattern suggests spinal cord compression
options.rationale: New severe back pain followed by weakness or sensory change in a patient with known metastatic disease is cord compression until proven otherwise. It is time dependent: function lost before treatment often does not come back. Treating the pain and waiting an hour spends the window the patient has.

options.text: Administer the ordered analgesic and reassess in an hour
options.rationale: Correct but premature Correct comfort care at exactly the wrong moment.

options.text: Apply heat to the back and reposition for comfort
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Comfort offered in place of escalation.

options.text: Encourage ambulation to assess the leg weakness
options.rationale: Near miss concept Risks a fall and delays imaging.

questions.takeaway: Back pain then weakness, in a cancer patient, is an emergency on a clock.
questions.strategy: A pain intervention is the wrong answer when the pain is the warning sign of a neurologic emergency.

questions.stem: During a vesicant chemotherapy infusion a patient reports burning at the intravenous site and the nurse notes swelling. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the infusion and leave the catheter in place
options.rationale: Extravasation of a vesicant causes tissue necrosis, so every second of continued infusion adds damage. Stop first. The catheter stays because the protocol often calls for aspirating residual drug through it and instilling an antidote. Flushing pushes more vesicant into the tissue.

options.text: Slow the infusion and apply a warm compress
options.rationale: Near miss concept Slowing still infuses, and the compress choice depends on the specific drug.

options.text: Flush the line with saline first to confirm that it is patent
options.rationale: Near miss concept Drives more vesicant into tissue that is already burning.

options.text: Remove the catheter and apply firm pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct for an ordinary infiltration, and here it discards the route the antidote needs.

questions.takeaway: Stop the infusion, keep the catheter. That line is now the treatment route.
questions.strategy: This is the one infiltration where you do not pull the catheter straight out.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes into the first infusion of a monoclonal antibody, a patient develops chills, flushing, a blood pressure of 88/50 and expiratory wheezing. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and continue to monitor
options.rationale: Near miss concept Appropriate for a mild reaction to some agents, not for bronchospasm with hypotension.

options.text: Administer an antihistamine per protocol
options.rationale: Correct but premature Treatment while the trigger is still infusing.

options.text: Obtain a set of vital signs and notify the provider
options.rationale: Correct but premature The stem already gave you the vital signs.

options.text: Stop the infusion
options.rationale: A reaction to a monoclonal antibody typically appears in the first 30 minutes to 2 hours and can include fever, chills, rash, hypotension and bronchospasm. The first action is to stop the infusion, because everything else happens while the causative agent is still entering the bloodstream.

questions.takeaway: When the drug is causing the reaction, stopping the drug is the first action.
questions.strategy: In any infusion reaction item, look for the option that removes the cause rather than treats the effect.

questions.stem: A patient with lung cancer develops facial and neck swelling, distended neck and chest veins and a hoarse voice. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and escalate immediately
options.rationale: This is superior vena cava syndrome: the tumor is compressing the vena cava and venous return from the head and arms is obstructed. Raising the head uses gravity to reduce the congestion while you escalate. The danger is airway compromise, so hoarseness and stridor make it emergent.

options.text: Place the patient flat to improve venous return
options.rationale: Near miss concept Worsens the congestion it claims to fix.

options.text: Measure neck circumference and document the finding
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Quantifies an emergency instead of escalating it.

options.text: Apply cool compresses to the face to reduce the swelling
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats the appearance of an obstruction.

questions.takeaway: Head up, escalate. The airway is what kills in this one.
questions.strategy: Any option that lays this patient flat is wrong, and so is any option that measures instead of acting.

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a white blood cell count of 1,200 per microliter. He is afebrile and reports feeling well. Which nursing action has the highest priority?

options.text: Implement neutropenic precautions and screen for subtle signs of infection
options.rationale: In neutropenia, infection is the deadliest risk and the usual signs may be absent because there are too few neutrophils to produce them. In an older or profoundly neutropenic patient, infection must be suspected even without a fever. Bleeding precautions address platelets, which is a different cell line.

options.text: Encourage a diet high in protein and calories to support marrow recovery
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Supportive and not the priority risk.

options.text: Reassure the patient that the absence of fever indicates no infection is present
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Uses a blunted response as evidence of safety.

options.text: Monitor for bleeding and institute bleeding precautions
options.rationale: Near miss concept Right idea, wrong cell line. The stem gave a white count.

questions.takeaway: No fever in neutropenia is not reassurance. It can mean the patient cannot mount one.
questions.strategy: Match the precaution to the cell line the stem actually gave you.

questions.stem: A patient on chemotherapy has an absolute neutrophil count of 400 and a single temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius. He looks well and has no localizing symptoms. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply protective precautions and reassess the patient in the morning
options.rationale: Correct but premature Precautions are appropriate and the delay is not.

options.text: Recheck the temperature in one hour to confirm it before acting
options.rationale: Correct but premature The threshold is a single reading; rechecking spends the hour.

options.text: Treat it as an emergency: cultures, then antibiotics within the hour
options.rationale: Febrile neutropenia is one fever in a patient with no neutrophils, and it is an oncologic emergency regardless of how well he looks, because he has no capacity to contain an infection or to show you where it is. Cultures and broad spectrum antibiotics go in within the hour. Giving an antipyretic masks the only sign he can still produce.

options.text: Give acetaminophen for the fever and continue to monitor him closely
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removes the only sign he can mount.

questions.takeaway: One temperature plus neutropenia is an emergency. Looking well means nothing here.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option buys time, and this is the patient with the least of it.

questions.topic: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage
