questions.stem: Patient A has a grade 1, stage IV tumor. Patient B has a grade 3, stage I tumor. Which statement is most accurate?
questions.objective: Differentiate tumor grade from cancer stage

options.text: Patient B's cancer is the more advanced one because poorly differentiated cells have already spread
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Grade describes the cells, not how far the cancer has spread.

options.text: Both tumors are equally advanced because the numbers add to the same total
options.rationale: Near miss concept Grade and stage are separate scales and are never combined.

options.text: Patient A's tumor is more aggressive because stage IV is the highest number
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stage IV means distant spread, not that the cells are more aggressive.

options.text: Patient A's cancer has spread further even though its cells look more like normal tissue
options.rationale: Grade describes how abnormal the cells look under a microscope: grade 1 cells resemble normal tissue, grade 3 cells are poorly differentiated. Stage describes how far the cancer has spread: stage IV is distant metastasis. A well differentiated tumor can still be widely spread.

questions.takeaway: Grade is the cells. Stage is the spread.
questions.strategy: Assign each number to its own scale.

questions.topic: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads
questions.stem: A patient who has smoked for 20 years asks, "Is there any point in quitting now? The damage is done." Which response reflects how cancer develops?
questions.objective: Explain how cancer develops, invades nearby tissue, and spreads

options.text: "Quitting lowers lung cancer risk only if it happens before any cell damage starts."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Initiated cells still need promotion to become cancer, so quitting later still helps.

options.text: "Yes. Quitting reverses the damage to the cell DNA within a few years."
options.rationale: Absolute language Initiation damage to DNA is permanent; what changes is the promotion.

options.text: "Quitting mainly helps the heart; the cancer risk is already fixed."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cancer risk is not fixed; it falls over time after quitting.

options.text: "Yes. Changes that have started can still be slowed when the promoter is removed."
options.rationale: Initiation is a permanent change to cell DNA. Promotion is the repeated exposure that pushes initiated cells to divide, and it can be slowed or stopped when the promoter, such as tobacco, is removed. That is why risk falls after quitting at any age.

questions.takeaway: Initiation is permanent; promotion is reversible.
questions.strategy: Ask which phase the action affects.

questions.topic: Plan patient and caregiver teaching for symptom management, follow up, and survivorship
questions.stem: Six years after finishing chemotherapy that included doxorubicin, a patient reports new fatigue, ankle swelling and shortness of breath when climbing stairs. What should the nurse teach?
questions.objective: Plan patient and caregiver teaching for symptom management, follow up, and survivorship

options.text: These may be late effects of treatment on the heart and need evaluation
options.rationale: Survivorship care includes late effects that appear years after treatment. Doxorubicin can damage the heart muscle and cause heart failure long after the last dose. New fatigue, edema and exertional dyspnea need evaluation, and survivors are taught to report them.

options.text: Fatigue after cancer is common and improves with rest and pacing
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Cancer related fatigue is real, but swelling and breathlessness point to the heart.

options.text: These symptoms most likely mean the cancer has returned
options.rationale: Most dramatic finding Recurrence is the feared answer, but this pattern fits a known late effect.

options.text: Ankle swelling is expected with aging and can be managed with leg elevation
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Treating the findings as normal aging misses heart failure.

questions.takeaway: Survivors: late effects can appear years later.
questions.strategy: Match the symptom cluster to the treatment history.

questions.topic: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response
questions.stem: A patient with breast cancer and bone metastasis reports back pain that is worse lying down, new constipation and difficulty starting urination. The calcium level is 10.2 mg/dL. Which emergency do these findings point to?
questions.objective: Recognize oncologic emergencies and prioritize the initial nursing response

options.text: Tumor lysis syndrome
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tumor lysis follows treatment and shows as electrolyte changes.

options.text: Superior vena cava syndrome
options.rationale: Near miss concept That causes facial and arm swelling, not back pain.

options.text: Spinal cord compression
options.rationale: Back pain worse lying down is often the first sign of spinal cord compression from vertebral metastasis. Bowel and bladder changes mean the cord is already affected. It is an emergency because delay leads to permanent paralysis; the provider is notified at once.

options.text: Hypercalcemia of malignancy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Constipation fits hypercalcemia, but the calcium is normal and back pain with urinary retention points to the cord.

questions.takeaway: Back pain plus bowel or bladder change: think cord compression.
questions.strategy: Rule out the look alike with the lab value given.

questions.topic: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment
questions.stem: A patient received IV cyclophosphamide 12 hours ago. Select all of the precautions the nurse should take.
questions.objective: Apply safety precautions when caring for patients receiving cancer treatment

options.text: Wear only standard exam gloves since urine is not the drug
options.rationale: Near miss concept Urine contains active drug and metabolites for about 48 hours.

options.text: Keep visitors out of the room for 48 hours
options.rationale: Near miss concept Chemotherapy does not make the patient a hazard to visitors.

options.text: Wash soiled linens separately from other laundry
options.rationale: Many chemotherapy drugs are excreted in urine, stool and other body fluids for about 48 hours. Staff wear a gown and double chemotherapy gloves to handle body fluids, flush with the lid closed, launder soiled linens separately and discard gloves in hazardous waste. Visitors are not restricted.

options.text: Remove the gloves and discard them in a regular trash container
options.rationale: Near miss concept Contaminated gloves go in a hazardous drug waste container.

options.text: Wear a gown and double chemotherapy gloves to empty the urinal
options.rationale: Many chemotherapy drugs are excreted in urine, stool and other body fluids for about 48 hours. Staff wear a gown and double chemotherapy gloves to handle body fluids, flush with the lid closed, launder soiled linens separately and discard gloves in hazardous waste. Visitors are not restricted.

options.text: Flush the toilet with the lid closed after disposing of urine
options.rationale: Many chemotherapy drugs are excreted in urine, stool and other body fluids for about 48 hours. Staff wear a gown and double chemotherapy gloves to handle body fluids, flush with the lid closed, launder soiled linens separately and discard gloves in hazardous waste. Visitors are not restricted.

questions.takeaway: Chemotherapy body fluids: 48 hours of hazardous drug precautions.
questions.strategy: Separate fluid exposure from contact with the patient.

questions.stem: Classify how each therapy is being used.

rows.text: Yoga used together with a prescribed anti inflammatory drug for chronic pain
Yoga and meditation used instead of the prescribed pain medication
An oncology team that plans acupuncture, massage and chemotherapy together as one coordinated plan
Traditional Chinese medicine used as the only system of care
Guided imagery added to a postoperative analgesic

questions.takeaway: Complementary therapies are used alongside conventional treatment. Alternative therapies replace conventional treatment and become the primary treatment. Integrative care deliberately coordinates conventional and complementary therapies around the whole person, with the patient and provider as partners. A whole medical system used in place of biomedicine is always alternative. Alongside, instead of, coordinated together.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the therapy is added, substituted or planned as one system.

questions.stem: What makes a therapy alternative rather than complementary?

options.text: It comes from a culture outside North America
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism Origin does not decide the label; how it is used does.

options.text: It requires special training to perform
options.rationale: Near miss concept Training requirements separate nursing accessible from training specific therapies.

options.text: It has not been studied in clinical trials
options.rationale: Near miss concept Evidence level does not define the category.

options.text: It is used in place of conventional treatment
options.rationale: The same therapy can be either. Yoga added to prescribed analgesics is complementary; yoga used instead of the medication is alternative. The deciding factor is whether it replaces biomedical care.

questions.takeaway: Alternative means instead of.
questions.strategy: Look for how the therapy is used, not what it is.

questions.stem: Select all of the features of integrative health care.

options.text: Focuses on the whole person, not only the disease
options.rationale: Integrative care is whole person, relationship based and evidence informed. It brings conventional and complementary therapies together rather than choosing one over the other.

options.text: Treats the patient and provider as equal partners
options.rationale: Integrative care is whole person, relationship based and evidence informed. It brings conventional and complementary therapies together rather than choosing one over the other.

options.text: Leaves the choice of therapies entirely to the provider
options.rationale: Near miss concept Integrative care is a partnership with the patient.

options.text: Replaces medications with natural products
options.rationale: Near miss concept Replacing conventional care is alternative, not integrative.

options.text: Combines conventional and complementary therapies
options.rationale: Integrative care is whole person, relationship based and evidence informed. It brings conventional and complementary therapies together rather than choosing one over the other.

options.text: Uses evidence to guide which therapies are chosen
options.rationale: Integrative care is whole person, relationship based and evidence informed. It brings conventional and complementary therapies together rather than choosing one over the other.

questions.takeaway: Integrative: whole person, partnership, both together.
questions.strategy: Reject options that replace care or exclude the patient.

questions.stem: Why do many patients seek complementary therapies?

options.text: Insurance plans usually require a trial of complementary therapy before any medication is covered
options.rationale: Institution as rationale Coverage rules are not the reason given.

options.text: Providers rarely prescribe medication for chronic disease
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Providers do prescribe for chronic disease; the gap is symptom and whole person care.

options.text: Conventional care does less for stress related illness, chronic symptoms and emotional needs
options.rationale: Biomedicine works well for infections and structural problems but is less effective for stress induced illness, chronic symptoms, emotional and spiritual needs and quality of life. Patients also report fewer unpleasant side effects with some therapies.

options.text: Complementary therapies are always safer than prescription drugs
options.rationale: Absolute language Natural does not mean safe; herbs can be toxic or interact with drugs.

questions.takeaway: Patients fill the gaps biomedicine leaves.
questions.strategy: Reject the absolute safety claim.

questions.stem: Classify each therapy as one a nurse can use independently or one that requires additional training or certification.

rows.text: Guided imagery
Acupuncture
Slow abdominal breathing
Biofeedback
Chiropractic manipulation
Progressive relaxation

questions.takeaway: Nursing accessible therapies use natural processes such as breathing, concentration, presence and movement: relaxation, meditation, breathwork, imagery, simple touch and music. Training specific therapies need postgraduate education, certification or licensure: acupuncture, biofeedback, therapeutic massage, acupressure and therapeutic touch. Chiropractic therapy is not a nursing therapy. Breathing, imagery, relaxation: nurse. Needles, devices, manipulation: trained.
questions.strategy: Ask whether a basic nurse could learn it at the bedside.

questions.stem: What determines which complementary therapies a nurse may perform?

options.text: The patient's preference alone
options.rationale: Near miss concept Preference matters for choice but does not set the nurse's scope.

options.text: Whether the therapy is popular in the community
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Popularity does not define scope.

options.text: Whether the therapy can be bought over the counter without a prescription
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Retail availability does not define scope.

options.text: The state nurse practice act and the nurse's training
options.rationale: Nurses practice only within their state nurse practice act and their training. Training specific therapies require certification beyond the registered nurse license.

questions.takeaway: Scope comes from the practice act and training.
questions.strategy: Pick the legal boundary.

questions.stem: Match each therapy to its category.

rows.text: Chiropractic spinal manipulation
Biofeedback
Probiotics
Ayurveda
Pilates
Guided imagery

questions.takeaway: Mind body therapies use thoughts and emotion to influence the body: imagery, meditation, biofeedback, breathwork, music and art. Body based therapies manipulate body structures: massage, chiropractic, acupressure. Movement therapies include Pilates, dance and Feldenkrais. Biologically based therapies are natural products: herbs, supplements, probiotics, special diets. Whole medical systems such as traditional Chinese medicine, Ayurveda, homeopathy and naturopathy are complete systems of theory and practice. Mind, body, movement, product, whole system.
questions.strategy: Ask what the therapy works through.

questions.stem: Which statement about whole medical systems is correct?

options.text: They are single herbal products that a patient uses to relieve one specific symptom
options.rationale: Near miss concept A single herb is a biologically based therapy.

options.text: They are always used alongside conventional care
options.rationale: Absolute language When used in place of biomedicine they are alternative.

options.text: They are exercise programs that build core strength
options.rationale: Near miss concept That describes Pilates, a movement therapy.

options.text: They are complete systems of theory and practice separate from biomedicine
options.rationale: Whole medical systems such as traditional Chinese medicine, Ayurveda, naturopathy and homeopathy have their own theory of health and illness. Used in place of biomedicine, they are always considered alternative because they rest on different philosophies.

questions.takeaway: Whole system: its own theory of health.
questions.strategy: Look for the word complete.

questions.stem: Match each whole medical system to its central idea.

rows.text: Balances the doshas through diet, herbs, massage and meditation
Uses tiny, highly diluted doses of substances that cause similar symptoms
Balances yin and yang and the flow of qi
Supports the body's own capacity for self healing

questions.takeaway: Traditional Chinese medicine balances yin and yang and qi along meridians. Ayurveda, from India, balances the doshas. Naturopathy treats the whole person and supports self healing. Homeopathy gives small, highly diluted doses of substances that would cause similar symptoms in a healthy person. Qi, doshas, self healing, like cures like.
questions.strategy: Match the system to its key word.

questions.stem: Classify each finding as part of the stress response or the relaxation response.

rows.text: Increased peripheral skin temperature
Lower blood pressure
Dilated pupils and tight muscles
Decreased oxygen consumption
Elevated blood glucose
Increased heart and respiratory rates

questions.takeaway: The stress response raises heart rate, respirations, blood pressure, muscle tension, metabolic rate, pupil size and blood glucose and lipids. The relaxation response lowers heart rate, respirations, blood pressure and oxygen consumption and raises peripheral skin temperature as vessels dilate. Stress speeds up; relaxation slows down and warms the skin.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the body is preparing to fight or settling down.

questions.stem: Why is chronic stress harmful even though the stress response is protective?

options.text: Chronic stress slows the heart rate to unsafe levels
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stress raises heart rate.

options.text: The stress response only occurs during physical danger
options.rationale: Near miss concept Thoughts and emotions trigger it too.

options.text: Sustained arousal raises the risk of hypertension, heart disease, anxiety and poor sleep
options.rationale: Short term, the stress response prepares the body to respond. Long term, it is maladaptive and contributes to anxiety, depression, digestive problems, headaches, muscle tension, heart disease, stroke, hypertension, sleep problems, weight gain and poor concentration.

options.text: Over time the stress response lowers blood glucose, which leads to repeated fainting spells
options.rationale: Near miss concept Stress raises blood glucose.

questions.takeaway: Protective short term, harmful long term.
questions.strategy: Look for the long term consequence.

questions.stem: Select all of the cognitive skills a patient develops through relaxation practice.

options.text: Receptivity, tolerating uncertain or unfamiliar experiences
options.rationale: Relaxation builds three cognitive skills: focusing, passivity and receptivity. The long term goal is for the person to notice tension and consciously release it.

options.text: Focusing attention on a simple stimulus for an extended time
options.rationale: Relaxation builds three cognitive skills: focusing, passivity and receptivity. The long term goal is for the person to notice tension and consciously release it.

options.text: Limiting what comes into the field of vision
options.rationale: Near miss concept Narrowing stimuli describes meditation, not a relaxation skill.

options.text: Building relationships with significant others
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Relationships are not one of the cognitive skills.

options.text: Passivity, stopping unnecessary goal directed activity
options.rationale: Relaxation builds three cognitive skills: focusing, passivity and receptivity. The long term goal is for the person to notice tension and consciously release it.

options.text: Solving problems faster under pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Passivity means stopping analytic problem solving.

questions.takeaway: Focus, passivity, receptivity.
questions.strategy: Pick the three inward skills.

questions.stem: How does passive relaxation differ from progressive relaxation?

options.text: Passive relaxation requires the patient to tense each muscle group harder
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tensing and releasing is progressive relaxation.

options.text: Passive relaxation must be led by a certified therapist
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Both are nursing accessible.

options.text: Passive relaxation is done only while the patient is asleep
options.rationale: Near miss concept The patient is awake and focused on breathing and warmth.

options.text: Passive relaxation stills the body without tensing and releasing muscle groups
options.rationale: Progressive relaxation tightens and releases an ordered succession of muscle groups with slow abdominal breathing. Passive relaxation uses slow breathing while imagining warmth flowing through body parts, with no muscle contraction, so it uses less energy.

questions.takeaway: Progressive tenses; passive does not.
questions.strategy: Ask whether muscles are contracted.

questions.stem: Place the steps for guiding progressive muscle relaxation in order.

options.text: Tighten one muscle group, such as the face, and hold the tension
Begin slow, deep abdominal breathing
Move to the next muscle group and repeat down the body
Release the tension and notice the difference between tension and relaxation
Help the patient into a comfortable position in a quiet setting

questions.takeaway: Prepare a quiet, comfortable setting, start slow abdominal breathing, then tense and release one muscle group at a time, noticing the contrast, and move in order through the body, from face to feet or feet to face. Settle, breathe, tense, release, move on.
questions.strategy: The breathing comes before the first muscle group.

questions.stem: Which patient is the poorest candidate for active progressive relaxation?

options.text: A patient with mild anxiety before a dental procedure
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Progressive relaxation suits mild anxiety.

options.text: A patient with chronic back pain who walks daily
options.rationale: Strength read as deficit Daily walking suggests adequate energy.

options.text: A patient with advanced cancer and very low energy reserves
options.rationale: Active progressive relaxation takes a moderate expenditure of energy and can increase fatigue. Patients with advanced disease or low energy reserves do better with passive relaxation or guided imagery.

options.text: A patient with tension headaches that start during stressful weeks of school exams
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data This patient has the energy for active relaxation.

questions.takeaway: Low energy: passive relaxation or imagery.
questions.strategy: Find the patient who cannot afford the effort.

questions.stem: Select all of the features of meditation.

options.rationale: The five features of meditation are a quiet space, a comfortable position, a receptive attitude, a focus of attention and relaxed breathing. It directs attention to a single unchanging or repetitive stimulus.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for surgery tomorrow takes valerian nightly for sleep. Why is this important to report?

options.text: Valerian raises blood pressure during surgery
options.rationale: Near miss concept Valerian is a central nervous system depressant, not a stimulant.

options.text: Valerian causes high blood glucose
options.rationale: Near miss concept Glucose is not the concern.

options.text: Valerian is a stimulant that keeps patients awake after anesthesia wears off
options.rationale: Near miss concept It depresses the central nervous system.

options.text: Valerian adds to sedation from anesthesia and opioids
options.rationale: Valerian depresses the central nervous system and adds to barbiturates, sleep aids, alcohol, antihistamines, anesthesia and opioids. Preoperative assessment always includes natural products.

questions.takeaway: Valerian sedates; report it before surgery.
questions.strategy: Ask what adds to anesthesia.

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia is anxious and short of breath. Oxygen saturation is 85%. The patient asks the nurse to lead a breathing exercise to calm down. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen per protocol
options.rationale: An oxygen saturation of 85% needs immediate respiratory intervention. Anxiety here is likely caused by hypoxemia. Once oxygenation is addressed and the provider notified, breathing exercises can support the patient.

options.text: Lead a slow abdominal breathing exercise
options.rationale: Correct but premature Relaxation does not correct hypoxemia and delays treatment.

options.text: Begin guided imagery of a calm beach
options.rationale: Correct but premature Imagery is not the priority while the patient is hypoxic.

options.text: Offer calming music, dim the lights and stay at the bedside
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Comforting, but it ignores the airway and breathing problem.

questions.takeaway: Hypoxia first, relaxation second.
questions.strategy: Apply the ABCs before comfort measures.

questions.stem: A patient on the first postoperative day rates pain 6 out of 10 and says, "I'm so anxious I can't relax." Analgesia is due now. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the analgesic and add guided imagery or slow breathing
options.rationale: Complementary therapies work with conventional treatment. The analgesic treats the pain, and imagery or breathing reduces anxiety and may reduce opioid use. The nurse reassesses pain and anxiety after both.

options.text: Teach guided imagery instead of giving the analgesic
options.rationale: Near miss concept Using imagery instead of the analgesic is alternative care, which undertreats pain.

options.text: Hold the analgesic until the patient tries meditation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Withholding ordered analgesia is unsafe.

options.text: Tell the patient that anxiety after surgery is normal and will pass on its own soon
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Reassurance does not treat pain or anxiety.

questions.takeaway: Complementary means added, not instead.
questions.strategy: Keep the prescribed treatment and add the therapy.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced heart failure is exhausted and anxious and asks for help relaxing. Which technique should the nurse offer?

options.text: Passive relaxation with slow breathing
options.rationale: Patients with low energy reserves do better with passive relaxation or guided imagery, which need no muscle contraction.

options.text: Active progressive muscle relaxation
options.rationale: Near miss concept Tensing muscles uses energy this patient lacks.

options.text: A vigorous yoga session
options.rationale: Near miss concept Too much exertion for advanced disease.

options.text: A brisk walk around the unit to release tension
options.rationale: Near miss concept Increases oxygen demand.

questions.takeaway: Low energy: passive relaxation.
questions.strategy: Match the effort to the energy.

questions.stem: A patient practicing progressive relaxation for several weeks reports new chest tightness during sessions. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Fully assess the new symptom and notify the provider
options.rationale: Early in training, patients may notice tension more. New or worsening symptoms may signal disease progression or a new illness, so the nurse assesses completely and notifies the provider.

options.text: Tell the patient increased awareness of tension is expected
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Increased tension awareness is expected early, but a new symptom is not.

options.text: Have the patient practice twice as long
options.rationale: Near miss concept More practice ignores a possible new problem.

options.text: Switch to guided imagery and continue
options.rationale: Correct but premature Changing technique before assessing misses the cause.

questions.takeaway: New symptom during relaxation: assess and report.
questions.strategy: Separate the expected from the new.

questions.stem: A patient with hypertension has meditated daily for three months. Blood pressure readings are now 98/60 and the patient feels lightheaded on standing. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the patient to skip the antihypertensive dose until the readings return to normal
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Only the provider changes the medication.

options.text: Document the improved readings as a success
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documenting does not address symptomatic low blood pressure.

options.text: Report the readings to the provider for a dose review
options.rationale: Prolonged meditation can reduce the need for antihypertensive medication. Low readings with lightheadedness mean the provider needs to review the dose. The nurse also teaches fall safety when standing.

options.text: Tell the patient to stop meditating
options.rationale: Near miss concept Meditation is helping; the medication may now be too strong.

questions.takeaway: Therapy working plus low blood pressure: provider adjusts the dose.
questions.strategy: Report, do not stop the therapy or the drug.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of physical abuse is anxious before a procedure. Which complementary therapy is the best choice?

options.text: Massage of the shoulders
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hands on therapy may trigger distress.

options.text: Holding the patient's hand without asking
options.rationale: Near miss concept Touch without permission is never appropriate.

options.text: Guided imagery with slow breathing
options.rationale: Patients with trauma may misinterpret touch and feel threatened. Imagery and breathing offer relaxation without touch. Assessing for trauma comes before choosing a touch therapy.

options.text: Therapeutic touch
options.rationale: Near miss concept Touch therapies may feel threatening after abuse.

questions.takeaway: Trauma history: choose a no touch therapy.
questions.strategy: Ask which option avoids touch.

questions.stem: A patient taking apixaban asks whether acupuncture could help chronic neck pain. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You can stop the apixaban for a few days before each session."
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Stopping an anticoagulant is a provider decision.

options.text: "Acupuncture has no evidence for pain relief."
options.rationale: Near miss concept There is evidence for neck and back pain.

options.text: "It may help, but apixaban raises bleeding risk. Let's involve your provider."
options.rationale: Acupuncture is effective for many types of pain, but anticoagulants raise bleeding risk at the needle sites. The nurse supports the choice, involves the provider and teaches the patient to disclose all medications to the practitioner.

options.text: "Acupuncture is never safe for anyone with neck pain."
options.rationale: Absolute language Absolute and inaccurate.

questions.takeaway: Needles plus anticoagulant: involve the provider.
questions.strategy: Choose accurate, supportive and collaborative.

questions.stem: A patient from a Chinese cultural background uses herbal teas from a traditional practitioner along with prescribed digoxin. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the patient to stop taking the digoxin while using the traditional herbal teas
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope The nurse does not stop prescribed drugs.

options.text: Ask about every tea and remedy and share the list with the provider
options.rationale: Many Chinese herbs interact with cardiovascular drugs. Patients often think of teas and powders as food, not medicine. The nurse asks about the full range of therapies respectfully and shares them with the provider.

options.text: Tell the patient to stop the teas because they are unregulated
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Dismissing the practice damages trust; the provider reviews interactions.

options.text: Ignore the teas because they are not medications
options.rationale: Near miss concept Patients may not see teas as medicine, but they can interact.

questions.takeaway: Ask about teas and powders too.
questions.strategy: Respect the culture and check the interactions.

questions.stem: A patient with new right lower abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting says, "I'm going to try herbal tea and meditation before seeing a doctor." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Suggest peppermint tea for the nausea
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Treating a symptom ignores the possible cause.

options.text: Teach progressive relaxation for the pain
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Relaxation does not treat appendicitis.

options.text: Urge prompt provider evaluation, since this may be appendicitis
options.rationale: Nurses advise patients when to seek conventional care. Acute right lower abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting may be appendicitis. A diagnosed chronic problem such as irritable bowel syndrome is where relaxation and herbs may help.

options.text: Support the plan because complementary therapy is usually safer than surgery or medication
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Supporting delay could miss a surgical emergency.

questions.takeaway: Acute new symptoms: conventional care first.
questions.strategy: Separate acute from chronic.

questions.stem: A patient had a first chiropractic treatment for chronic low back pain and is going home. Classify each teaching point.

rows.text: "Call the office if you have tingling or numbness in your hands or legs."
"If the pain returns today, place a 3 pound weight on your lower back."
"Plan to nap for 40 minutes when you get home."
"Keep track of how often you need pain medication and bring it to the next visit."

questions.takeaway: Numbness or tingling may signal nerve injury and must be reported. Weight on the back could cause harm. A nap makes no difference. Some patients need less pain medication after treatment, so tracking use helps the provider adjust doses. Report nerve symptoms; track medication need.
questions.strategy: Ask whether each point protects, harms or does nothing.

questions.stem: The nurse taught a patient creative visualization. Which statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I'll picture the worst outcome so I am prepared."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Negative images undo the purpose.

options.text: "I only need to try it once to see if it works."
options.rationale: Near miss concept Visualization requires frequent practice.

options.text: "I should use it only when my pain is severe."
options.rationale: Near miss concept It is practiced throughout the day, especially when relaxed.

options.text: "I'll picture my garden clearly, often, especially before bed."
options.rationale: Creative visualization uses a clear, pleasing image held in the present tense and practiced often, especially before bedtime or on waking, with encouraging statements. Teach back confirms understanding.

questions.takeaway: Clear, pleasant, present tense, practiced often.
questions.strategy: Pick the statement with frequent positive practice.

questions.stem: An older adult with a history of falls asks about an exercise to improve balance. Which recommendation is best?

options.text: A high impact aerobics class
options.rationale: Near miss concept High impact exercise increases fall risk.

options.text: A group tai chi class
options.rationale: Tai chi improves balance and reduces falls and fear of falling in older adults. Pilates, low impact and core focused, also improves balance and function.

options.text: Magnet therapy bracelets
options.rationale: Near miss concept Magnets do not improve balance.

options.text: Cupping therapy
options.rationale: Near miss concept Cupping does not improve balance.

questions.takeaway: Falls: tai chi.
questions.strategy: Pick the low impact balance option.

questions.stem: A patient says, "I've decided to stop chemotherapy and use only a macrobiotic diet and herbs." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Tell me more about what led you to this decision."
options.rationale: Using therapies in place of conventional care is alternative. The nurse explores the patient's reasons and goals without judgment, provides accurate information so the decision is informed and involves the provider. The patient has the right to decide.

options.text: "That is a dangerous choice and you need to reconsider."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Judgment closes the conversation.

options.text: "Natural treatments work just as well, so that is fine."
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic False reassurance is inaccurate.

options.text: "I will tell your oncologist you are refusing care."
options.rationale: Correct but premature The provider needs to know, but first understand the patient's reasons.

questions.takeaway: Explore first; inform, do not judge.
questions.strategy: Pick the open, therapeutic response.

questions.stem: A nurse gave guided imagery to a patient for procedure anxiety. Which finding best shows the therapy was effective?

options.text: Heart rate fell from 104 to 82 and the patient reports feeling calmer
options.rationale: Evaluation looks for the relaxation response: slower heart rate and respirations, lower blood pressure and the patient's report of calm.

options.text: The nurse finished the imagery script
options.rationale: Task completion as outcome Finishing the script is a task, not an outcome.

options.text: The patient's family thanked the nurse
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Gratitude does not measure the patient's response.

options.text: The patient fell asleep and could not be awakened easily before the procedure began
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Sleep may or may not reflect reduced anxiety.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate the patient's response.
questions.strategy: Pick measurable change in the patient.

questions.stem: On the advice of an Ayurvedic practitioner, a patient stops a prescribed antidepressant and uses herbs, yoga and dietary changes instead. Which description is most accurate?

options.text: Complementary care using mind body therapies
options.rationale: Near miss concept Yoga is mind body, but nothing is being added alongside the conventional treatment.

options.text: Integrative care using mind body therapies
options.rationale: Near miss concept Integrative care needs conventional treatment in the plan.

options.text: Alternative care using a whole medical system
options.rationale: When a therapy replaces conventional treatment, it is alternative. Ayurveda is a whole medical system, and whole systems used in place of biomedicine are always alternative.

options.text: Integrative care using a whole medical system
options.rationale: Near miss concept Integrative care coordinates both; here the prescribed drug was replaced.

questions.takeaway: Replaced, not added: alternative.
questions.strategy: Decide added or replaced before naming the category.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure takes digoxin and furosemide and has started licorice root for indigestion. Which assessment is the priority?

options.text: Blood glucose
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Glucose is not affected in this combination.

options.text: Liver enzymes
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Liver enzymes are not the concern with licorice.

options.text: Potassium level
options.rationale: Licorice root lowers potassium, and furosemide does too. Low potassium makes digoxin more toxic, raising the risk of dysrhythmias. The nurse checks the potassium level and assesses for signs of digoxin toxicity.

options.text: Blood pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Licorice interacts with antihypertensives, but the danger with digoxin is potassium.

questions.takeaway: Licorice plus a loop diuretic plus digoxin: check potassium.
questions.strategy: Follow the interaction to the most dangerous effect.

questions.stem: A patient with generalized anxiety disorder has meditated daily for four months and says, "I feel so much calmer that I stopped my alprazolam three days ago." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Meditation can reduce the need for antianxiety drugs, so that is reasonable"
options.rationale: Near miss concept The dose may come down, but stopping a benzodiazepine abruptly can cause withdrawal.

options.text: "Keep meditating, and call if your anxiety comes back"
options.rationale: Correct but premature It ignores the withdrawal risk of stopping suddenly.

options.text: "Stop meditating until your provider reviews your medications"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Meditation is helping and does not need to stop.

options.text: "Restart it as prescribed and talk with your provider about tapering"
options.rationale: Prolonged meditation can reduce the need for psychotropic medications, but the provider adjusts doses. Stopping a benzodiazepine abruptly can cause withdrawal and seizures, so the patient restarts it as prescribed and the provider plans any taper.

questions.takeaway: Therapy working: the provider adjusts the dose, never the patient alone.
questions.strategy: Keep the benefit and remove the danger.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of assault asks a nurse certified in therapeutic touch for a session to ease chronic pain. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain what the session involves, get consent and keep it brief and gentle
options.rationale: Patients with trauma may misinterpret touch and feel threatened, so the nurse assesses first. When the patient understands and requests it, the nurse explains what will happen, gets consent, keeps the session gentle and time limited and stops if distress appears.

options.text: Decline the request because touch therapies are contraindicated for patients after trauma
options.rationale: Absolute language Trauma calls for caution, not automatic refusal of a requested therapy.

options.text: Offer guided imagery in place of touch and avoid discussing the request at all
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Substituting without discussion overrides the patient's choice.

options.text: Provide the full session as requested because the patient chose the therapy freely
options.rationale: Near miss concept The request does not remove the need to explain, consent and watch for distress.

questions.takeaway: Trauma and touch: inform, consent, go gently.
questions.strategy: Respect the request while adding safety.

questions.stem: During a preoperative assessment three days before surgery, a patient reports taking ginkgo and garlic capsules daily. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Document the supplements on the medication history
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Documenting is needed but does not get the bleeding risk addressed.

options.text: Check the platelet count before the day of surgery
options.rationale: Correct but premature A normal platelet count does not rule out the antiplatelet effect.

options.text: Report the supplements to the surgical provider
options.rationale: Ginkgo and garlic inhibit platelet function and increase bleeding during surgery. The nurse reports them to the surgical provider, who decides about stopping them or delaying surgery. A platelet count measures the number of platelets, not how well they work.

options.text: Tell the patient to stop both supplements today
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope The surgical team decides whether to stop the supplements or change the plan.

questions.takeaway: Bleeding herbs before surgery: tell the surgical team.
questions.strategy: Route the risk to the one who decides.

questions.stem: A patient becomes jaundiced with dark urine, and laboratory results show a rising unconjugated bilirubin and a falling hemoglobin. What is happening?

options.text: Slow bleeding into the gastrointestinal tract is lowering the counts
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blood loss drops the hemoglobin without the jaundice.

options.text: The liver has failed and can no longer conjugate or clear bilirubin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Liver failure can raise bilirubin and does not drop the hemoglobin this way.

options.text: The bone marrow has stopped producing enough new red blood cells
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would not raise bilirubin, since nothing is breaking down.

options.text: Red cells are breaking down faster than the marrow replaces them
options.rationale: Hemolysis dumps heme into the circulation. The liver cannot conjugate it fast enough, so unconjugated bilirubin rises and the patient yellows, while the breakdown products darken the urine. A reticulocyte count would be high, because the marrow is working hard to keep up, which is what separates destruction from a production failure.

questions.takeaway: Jaundice plus dark urine plus falling hemoglobin is destruction, not loss.
questions.strategy: The reticulocyte count is the question that separates these: high means destruction or loss, low means the marrow quit.

questions.stem: A patient with anemia has a very low reticulocyte count. What does this indicate?

options.text: A destruction problem, with cells lost faster than they are made
options.rationale: Near miss concept Destruction drives the count up, not down.

options.text: A recovering anemia, with the marrow now resting after a response
options.rationale: Near miss concept A rising reticulocyte count signals recovery; a low one signals the opposite.

options.text: Acute bleeding, with the marrow not yet signaled to respond
options.rationale: Near miss concept Bleeding raises the reticulocyte count as the marrow compensates.

options.text: A production problem, with the marrow not making new red cells
options.rationale: Reticulocytes are immature red cells, so the count tells you whether the marrow is responding. Low means the factory is down: marrow suppression, chemotherapy, missing erythropoietin, or missing building blocks. High means the marrow is working hard, which points to bleeding or hemolysis. It is the single most useful test for sorting anemias.

questions.takeaway: Low retics means the marrow quit. High retics means something is destroying or losing cells.
questions.strategy: This one value splits every anemia into two categories, which is why it is ordered.

questions.stem: Match each pattern to what it most suggests.

rows.text: Neutrophils below 1,000
Elevated eosinophils
Elevated lymphocytes
Elevated neutrophils

questions.takeaway: The differential tells you what the immune system is fighting. Neutrophils rise against bacteria, lymphocytes against viruses, eosinophils in allergy and parasitic disease. A neutrophil count under 1,000 is neutropenia, where infection becomes the deadliest risk and may arrive without a fever, especially in an older adult. A total white count can be normal while the differential is screaming. Read the parts.
questions.strategy: Ask which cell line moved, then ask what that cell line fights.

options.text: Black tarry stool
options.rationale: Platelet problems bleed into skin and mucosa, which is why petechiae, gum bleeding and unexplained bruising cluster together, and why a black tarry stool means he is bleeding somewhere you cannot see. questions.takeaway: Petechiae and mucosal bleeding point at platelets. Deep joint and muscle bleeding points at factors.

questions.stem: Select all of the nursing responsibilities during a red cell transfusion.

options.text: Stay with the patient and monitor closely during the first 15 minutes
options.rationale: The first fifteen minutes is when a hemolytic reaction declares itself, which is why you do not leave the room, and the slow start is deliberate. Blood runs with normal saline only; dextrose causes hemolysis and calcium containing solutions clot the line. Nothing is ever added to a blood product.

options.text: Obtain baseline vital signs immediately before starting
options.rationale: The first fifteen minutes is when a hemolytic reaction declares itself, which is why you do not leave the room, and the slow start is deliberate. Blood runs with normal saline only; dextrose causes hemolysis and calcium containing solutions clot the line. Nothing is ever added to a blood product.

options.text: Complete the infusion within the maximum time allowed by policy
options.rationale: The first fifteen minutes is when a hemolytic reaction declares itself, which is why you do not leave the room, and the slow start is deliberate. Blood runs with normal saline only; dextrose causes hemolysis and calcium containing solutions clot the line. Nothing is ever added to a blood product.

options.text: Prime and infuse the unit with dextrose 5 percent in water
options.rationale: Near miss concept Dextrose hemolyzes red cells; saline only.

options.text: Add the ordered premedication directly to the blood bag
options.rationale: Absolute language Nothing is added to a blood product.

options.text: Verify the unit against the order and the patient with a second qualified person
options.rationale: The first fifteen minutes is when a hemolytic reaction declares itself, which is why you do not leave the room, and the slow start is deliberate. Blood runs with normal saline only; dextrose causes hemolysis and calcium containing solutions clot the line. Nothing is ever added to a blood product.

questions.takeaway: Normal saline only, and stay for the first fifteen minutes. That is when it goes wrong.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options put the wrong substance into the blood or the line.

questions.stem: A patient's platelet count is 28,000. Select all of the precautions the nurse should implement.

questions.topic: sorting the anemias with one value
questions.stem: Four patients have a hemoglobin of 9.2. Which laboratory value would most efficiently separate a production problem from a loss or destruction problem?
questions.objective: sorting the anemias with one value

options.text: The mean corpuscular volume
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sorts micro from macrocytic, which subdivides production problems rather than separating the two categories.

options.text: The reticulocyte count
options.rationale: Reticulocytes are immature red cells, so the count tells you whether the marrow is responding. High means it is working hard, which points to bleeding or hemolysis. Low means the factory is down: marrow suppression, missing erythropoietin or missing building blocks. Cell size and ferritin narrow the production causes, and bilirubin only helps if hemolysis is the answer, so all three come after the first split.

options.text: The ferritin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Excellent for iron deficiency specifically, which is one production cause among several.

options.text: The total bilirubin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rises in hemolysis and is normal in blood loss, so it answers only part of the question.

questions.takeaway: One value splits every anemia in half. Order it first and the rest of the workup narrows.
questions.strategy: The question asks which is most efficient, not which is useful. Look for the one that sorts into two groups.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a hemoglobin of 8.6 g/dL. What explains the anemia?

options.text: The kidneys make too little erythropoietin to drive red cell production
options.rationale: Erythropoietin is made in the kidney and tells the marrow to build red cells. When kidney tissue is lost, that signal fades and production falls, which is a production problem rather than a loss or destruction problem. That is also why treatment is an erythropoiesis stimulating agent plus iron rather than transfusion alone.

options.text: The kidneys are destroying red blood cells as the blood is filtered
options.rationale: Near miss concept Destruction happens in the spleen and the circulation, not by filtration.

options.text: Reduced kidney function blocks iron absorption from the gut entirely
options.rationale: Near miss concept Iron absorption is a gut and hepcidin story; the kidney contributes the hormone.

options.text: The kidneys are losing large numbers of red blood cells in the urine
options.rationale: Near miss concept Hematuria occurs in some kidney disease and is not the mechanism of this anemia.

questions.takeaway: The kidney is an endocrine organ. Losing it costs you red cells.
questions.strategy: Sort anemias into production, loss and destruction. The kidney belongs to production.

questions.stem: A patient reports fatigue and a craving for ice. Laboratory results show a low hemoglobin with small, pale red cells and a low ferritin. What does this indicate?

options.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency
options.rationale: Near miss concept Macrocytic, with numbness, tingling and glossitis.

options.text: Anemia of chronic kidney disease
options.rationale: Near miss concept Usually normocytic, from an erythropoietin shortage rather than empty iron stores.

options.text: Iron deficiency anemia
options.rationale: Small and pale is microcytic hypochromic, which is the iron picture, and a low ferritin confirms the stores are empty. Pica, the craving for ice or clay or starch, is a classic and easily missed clue. B12 makes the cells large rather than small and brings neurologic signs. The next question is always where the iron went, which usually means looking for blood loss.

options.text: Hemolytic anemia
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would bring jaundice, dark urine and a high reticulocyte count.

questions.takeaway: Microcytic and hypochromic is iron. Macrocytic with neuropathy is B12.
questions.strategy: Cell size splits these: small for iron, large for B12 and folate.

questions.stem: A patient with anemia reports numbness and tingling in both feet, and the nurse notes a smooth, beefy red tongue. Which deficiency does this suggest?

options.text: Vitamin K
options.rationale: Near miss concept A clotting problem, not an anemia.

options.text: Vitamin B12
options.rationale: Neurologic symptoms are what separate B12 from every other anemia. B12 is needed for myelin, so deficiency brings numbness, tingling and gait problems, with glossitis in the mouth. Iron and folate deficiency make a person tired and pale without the neuropathy. Absorption requires intrinsic factor, which is why gastric surgery and pernicious anemia cause it.

options.text: Folate
options.rationale: Near miss concept Also macrocytic, and it spares the nerves, which is the classic discriminator from B12.

options.text: Iron
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fatigue, pallor and pica, and no neurologic findings.

questions.takeaway: Anemia plus neuropathy is B12 until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: Three anemias look alike until you ask about the feet.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has a platelet count of 62,000 and an international normalized ratio of 2.1. He has not received any anticoagulant. What explains both findings?

options.text: Vitamin K deficiency from poor intake is the sole cause of both
options.rationale: Near miss concept Contributes to the coagulopathy and explains neither the platelets nor the full picture.

options.text: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia from exposure during this stay
options.rationale: Near miss concept He has had no heparin, and it would not raise the international normalized ratio.

options.text: The liver cannot make clotting factors; the spleen holds platelets
options.rationale: Two separate mechanisms in one organ system. Clotting factors are synthesized in the liver, so a failing liver lengthens the prothrombin time and raises the international normalized ratio without any anticoagulant. Portal hypertension enlarges the spleen, and an enlarged spleen traps platelets. Both are expected in advanced cirrhosis and together they make him a serious bleeding risk.

options.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is consuming both of them
options.rationale: Near miss concept Would consume fibrinogen and raise D dimer, with clinical bleeding and clotting together.

questions.takeaway: The liver makes the factors and portal hypertension traps the platelets. Both at once.
questions.strategy: No heparin in the stem rules out one option on its face, which is the detail to look for.

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a white blood cell count of 1,200 with a low neutrophil fraction. He is afebrile and feels well. What is the nursing priority?

options.text: Implement neutropenic precautions and monitor for infection even without fever
options.rationale: Neutrophils are what generate a fever, so a neutropenic patient can be septic and afebrile. That makes absence of fever meaningless and makes subtle changes, a new confusion, a drop in pressure, a vague malaise, the signs you actually act on. Fresh produce is restricted on many neutropenic protocols, not encouraged.

options.text: Place the patient on bleeding precautions
options.rationale: Near miss concept That follows the platelet count, which the stem does not give.

options.text: Encourage fresh fruit and vegetables to support recovery
options.rationale: Near miss concept Raw produce carries organisms and is restricted on many neutropenic protocols.

options.text: Reassure the patient that being afebrile means there is no infection
options.rationale: Near miss concept Uses the one sign this patient cannot mount as evidence of safety.

questions.takeaway: No neutrophils, no fever. Waiting for a temperature is waiting for nothing.
questions.strategy: The afebrile detail is placed there to reassure you. It should do the opposite.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic anemia from kidney disease has a hemoglobin of 7.4. He is ambulating without dyspnea, has no chest pain, and his heart rate is 78. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Transfusion of two units today, since the hemoglobin is below 8
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treats a threshold, and two units is rarely the starting point even when transfusion is indicated.

options.text: Transfusion of one unit now, then reassessment of the hemoglobin
options.rationale: Near miss concept Correct practice when transfusion is indicated; he is asymptomatic and adapted.

options.text: No transfusion; expect erythropoiesis stimulating therapy and iron
options.rationale: A patient with chronic anemia has adapted over months, and he is asymptomatic at a number that would distress someone who dropped there in a day. Restrictive transfusion practice is the standard because transfusion carries real risks and, in kidney disease, repeated transfusion complicates future transplantation. Treat the cause, which is the missing erythropoietin, and transfuse for symptoms.

options.text: Transfusion only once the hemoglobin falls below 6 on a recheck
options.rationale: Near miss concept Another fixed threshold, in the other direction; symptoms decide.

questions.takeaway: Chronic anemia is tolerated far better than acute. Transfuse for symptoms, not for a threshold.
questions.strategy: A single numeric trigger is almost always the wrong answer in transfusion decisions.

questions.stem: A patient with a hemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL is short of breath at rest and has chest pain. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Observation with a repeat count in the morning
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Watches a patient with demand ischemia overnight.

options.text: Transfusion of packed red blood cells
options.rationale: Symptoms decide, not the number alone. A patient with angina and dyspnea at rest is not delivering enough oxygen to the heart muscle right now, and iron or erythropoietin take weeks to build cells. One unit raises the hemoglobin by roughly 1 g/dL. The cause still gets worked up afterward.

options.text: Oral iron supplementation and dietary teaching
options.rationale: Correct but premature Weeks to work, in a patient with chest pain now.

options.text: An erythropoiesis stimulating agent
options.rationale: Correct but premature Also weeks, and it needs iron available to work with.

questions.takeaway: Transfuse for symptoms, not for a number.
questions.strategy: Two options are correct treatments on a timescale this patient does not have.

questions.stem: A patient on heparin for five days has a platelet count that has fallen from 210,000 to 48,000. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the heparin and notify the provider immediately
options.rationale: A platelet drop of more than half after about five days of heparin is heparin induced thrombocytopenia. The counterintuitive part is that the danger is clotting, not bleeding: the antibodies activate the remaining platelets. Giving platelets adds fuel. The heparin stops and a non heparin anticoagulant takes over.

options.text: Recheck the platelet count in the morning to confirm the trend
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting The trend is already clear, and the delay is spent clotting.

options.text: Continue the heparin and institute bleeding precautions
options.rationale: Near miss concept Precautions are reasonable and the heparin is the cause.

options.text: Administer the ordered platelet transfusion
options.rationale: Near miss concept Feeds the clotting process in a patient whose problem is activation, not deficiency.

questions.takeaway: Low platelets on heparin means stop the heparin. The risk is thrombosis, not hemorrhage.
questions.strategy: The instinct to transfuse a low platelet count is exactly what this condition punishes.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 78 year old patient at a clinic visit. Which statement by the patient requires follow up?

options.text: My hair has been thinning slowly on my legs for years
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Slow, even hair loss on the legs is a normal aging change.

options.text: My skin gets drier in the winter
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Dry skin is common in older adults and is not a reliable sign of a blood problem.

options.text: I bruise more easily now that I am older
options.rationale: New or easier bruising is a bleeding tendency to evaluate, not an aging change. Compare with the patient's baseline and assess for a platelet or clotting problem.

options.text: I have had the same energy level as last year
options.rationale: Kind but non therapeutic Energy that matches the patient's own baseline is reassuring, not a finding to follow up.

questions.takeaway: Unexplained or easier bruising in an older adult is evaluated, not explained away by age. Slow leg hair loss and dry skin are expected.
questions.strategy: Find the statement that describes a change in bruising, bleeding, energy or infections; the patient's own explanation of aging does not make it normal.

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a platelet count of 22 K/µL this morning. The nurse reviews the note below. Select all of the findings that require follow up. Note: “0800. Alert and oriented. Pinpoint red spots scattered on both lower legs. Gums bleed when brushing teeth. Temperature 36.9 °C. Heart rate 84/min. Reports a new headache since last night, 7 of 10. Pink tinged urine in the urinal. Skin warm and dry. Ate 75% of breakfast.”

options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Normal mental status is reassuring. A change such as confusion would need follow up because it can signal bleeding in the brain.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: The nurse receives morning results for four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Taking warfarin, INR 2.6, no bleeding noted
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem An INR of 2.6 is within the usual warfarin goal of 2 to 3, and there is no bleeding. This result is therapeutic and expected.

options.text: Neutrophils low after chemotherapy, temperature 38.4 °C
options.rationale: Neutropenia carries the highest infection risk, and a fever here can mean a fast moving infection the body cannot fight. This is the unstable patient and is seen first.

options.text: Heparin infusion, aPTT twice the control value
options.rationale: Near miss concept An aPTT about 1.5 to 2.5 times the control value is the usual therapeutic range for unfractionated heparin. This result is on target.

options.text: Enoxaparin daily, no aPTT ordered this week
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Enoxaparin usually needs no routine clotting test, and the aPTT does not measure its effect. No aPTT is expected, not a problem.

questions.takeaway: Neutropenia carries the highest infection risk, so a fever in a neutropenic patient is urgent. Therapeutic INR and aPTT values are expected findings.
questions.strategy: Sort each patient as expected or unexpected. Three results are on target for their drug; only one shows a new problem in a high risk patient.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a patient going home on enoxaparin injections. Which patient statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: I will need an INR blood test every week
options.rationale: Absolute language INR monitors warfarin. Enoxaparin usually needs no routine clotting test, and INR and aPTT do not measure its effect.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient with pancytopenia after chemotherapy is admitted. The nurse reviews the admission findings. The nurse is admitting a patient with pancytopenia after chemotherapy. For each finding, indicate the risk it most directly signals.
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

rows.text: Hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL
Petechiae across the chest
Platelets 18 K/µL
Neutrophils 0.4 K/µL
Temperature 38.2 °C with chills
Short of breath walking to the bathroom

questions.takeaway: Low hemoglobin means less oxygen carrying protein, so tissues receive less oxygen. This is the anemia part of pancytopenia. Petechiae are pinpoint bleeds in tiny vessels and are a classic sign of thrombocytopenia. A very low platelet count means platelets cannot form the initial plug at vessel injuries, so bleeding risk is high. Neutropenia carries the highest infection vulnerability because neutrophils are the first responders to bacteria. A count this low means almost no first responders are available. Fever with chills in a patient with low WBCs signals infection, even if other signs of inflammation are muted. Dyspnea and activity intolerance are how anemia shows itself: the heart and lungs work harder to deliver oxygen with too few RBCs. Pancytopenia lowers all three cell lines, so assess for bleeding, infection and poor oxygen delivery at every encounter. Each finding points back to the cell line that is low.
questions.strategy: Link each finding to the cell that is missing: platelets mean bleeding, neutrophils mean infection, RBCs and hemoglobin mean oxygen delivery.

questions.topic: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests
questions.stem: Three hours after an iliac crest aspiration, a patient's platelets are 62 K/µL. A quarter size spot on the dressing is larger than 1 hour ago. What does the nurse do first?
questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

options.text: Give an aspirin free analgesic
options.rationale: Correct but premature Pain control matters, but the growing spot is active bleeding, which comes first.

options.text: Mark the spot and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Near miss concept Marking helps track drainage, but waiting an hour lets active bleeding continue in a patient with low platelets.

options.text: Change the dressing and assess the site
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removing the dressing disturbs the clot forming at the site and delays pressure.

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the site
options.rationale: Bleeding is the priority after a bone marrow procedure. A growing spot with low platelets is active bleeding, so pressure comes first, then the provider is notified.

questions.takeaway: After a bone marrow aspiration, bleeding is the priority. A growing spot on the dressing means active bleeding: apply firm pressure first.
questions.strategy: Spot the active problem (the spot is growing) and choose the action that stops it now.

questions.topic: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests
questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for a bone marrow aspiration at the posterior iliac crest with sedation this afternoon. Which actions does the nurse include before the procedure? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the iliac crest
options.rationale: Correct but premature Pressure is applied after the needle is removed, to control bleeding. It is not a preparation step.

options.text: Position the patient prone or side lying as ordered
options.rationale: Prone or side lying exposes the posterior iliac crest, the usual site. Fasting is needed for local anesthetic alone, but when sedation is planned the patient is kept NPO as ordered. Bleeding risks and anticoagulants are reviewed before the procedure; the provider decides whether to hold them.

options.text: Keep the patient NPO as ordered because sedation will be used
options.rationale: Prone or side lying exposes the posterior iliac crest, the usual site. Fasting is needed for local anesthetic alone, but when sedation is planned the patient is kept NPO as ordered. Bleeding risks and anticoagulants are reviewed before the procedure; the provider decides whether to hold them.

options.text: Ask the provider whether warfarin is to be held
options.rationale: Prone or side lying exposes the posterior iliac crest, the usual site. Fasting is needed for local anesthetic alone, but when sedation is planned the patient is kept NPO as ordered. Bleeding risks and anticoagulants are reviewed before the procedure; the provider decides whether to hold them.

options.text: Withhold all fluids for 24 hours beforehand
options.rationale: Absolute language NPO time follows the sedation order; a 24 hour fluid restriction is not standard and risks dehydration.

options.text: Give aspirin for comfort before the procedure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Aspirin blocks platelets and raises bleeding risk; it is avoided around the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Before a bone marrow aspiration with sedation: position prone or side lying, keep NPO as ordered, and review anticoagulants with the provider. Pressure comes after; aspirin is avoided.
questions.strategy: Sort each option by timing and safety: preparation steps before, site pressure after, and nothing that adds bleeding risk.

questions.topic: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health
questions.stem: A patient with new anemia gives this history. Which detail is most important for the nurse to follow up?
questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

options.text: Eats red meat about once a week
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diet matters for blood health, but eating some red meat weekly is not a strong cause of new anemia and is not an exposure risk.

options.text: Takes a daily multivitamin with iron
options.rationale: Near miss concept A multivitamin with iron supports RBC production. It does not explain the anemia and is not a hazard.

options.text: Cooks on a gas stove with a working CO alarm
options.rationale: Near miss concept Carbon monoxide impairs hemoglobin function but does not lower the hemoglobin count, and a working alarm lowers the risk. This does not explain anemia.

options.text: Has been stripping paint in a 1920s home
options.rationale: Disturbing older paint during renovation is a common source of lead exposure. Lead interferes with heme production and can cause anemia, so the nurse follows up and anticipates a blood lead test.

questions.takeaway: Ask about home, work and hobby exposures in every hematologic history. Old paint disturbed during renovation is a classic lead source, and lead blocks heme production.
questions.strategy: Match the problem to the exposure that causes it. Anemia means less hemoglobin is being made, so look for the exposure that blocks heme production.

questions.topic: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities
questions.stem: A patient found in a closed garage with a running generator is receiving 100% oxygen by nonrebreather. Which finding most indicates the need for escalation and possible hyperbaric oxygen?
questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

options.text: Headache rated 7 of 10
options.rationale: Near miss concept Headache is the most common symptom of carbon monoxide poisoning; by itself it does not mark severe poisoning.

options.text: Nausea and one episode of vomiting
options.rationale: Near miss concept Nausea and vomiting are common symptoms and do not on their own signal a severe exposure.

options.text: SpO2 of 99% on the nonrebreather
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Pulse oximetry can read falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning, so this number neither reassures nor signals severity.

options.text: New confusion that is getting worse
options.rationale: Worsening neurologic status, such as new confusion or loss of consciousness, signals severe poisoning and is escalated promptly; severe cases may need hyperbaric oxygen.

questions.takeaway: In carbon monoxide poisoning, neurologic changes such as new or worsening confusion or loss of consciousness mark severe poisoning and are escalated promptly. A normal SpO2 means nothing here.
questions.strategy: Separate common symptoms from signs of severity: the brain is the organ that shows a dangerous oxygen shortage.

questions.topic: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities
questions.stem: Three people from one household arrive at the emergency department in winter. They spent the night heating a closed room with a kerosene heater. The patient the nurse is assessing reports a throbbing headache, nausea and dizziness, and the other two have the same headache. Heart rate is 112/min. SpO2 is 98% on room air. Complete the bow tie.
questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

options.text: Give an antiemetic and encourage oral fluids
Apply 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask
Give oxygen at 2 L by nasal cannula
Notify the provider and expect a carboxyhemoglobin level
Titrate oxygen down to an SpO2 of 94%
Viral gastroenteritis
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Migraine headache
Influenza
Blood lead level
Pulse oximetry trend
Carboxyhemoglobin level
Hemoglobin level
Neurologic status and level of consciousness

questions.takeaway: 100% oxygen speeds removal of carbon monoxide from hemoglobin and is given right away, regardless of the SpO2 value. Prompt reporting is a priority, and a carboxyhemoglobin level confirms the diagnosis. Severe cases may need hyperbaric oxygen. Headache, nausea and dizziness in several people from one home heated by a fuel burning heater is the classic pattern. The SpO2 is falsely normal. This level confirms carbon monoxide poisoning and shows whether treatment is working as it falls. The brain is very sensitive to low oxygen. Confusion, seizures or loss of consciousness signal severe poisoning. Several people from one home with headache, nausea and dizziness near a fuel burning heater means carbon monoxide until proven otherwise. Give 100% oxygen, report promptly, and follow the carboxyhemoglobin level and neuro status, not the SpO2.
questions.strategy: Start with the condition: the shared symptoms and the heater make the pattern. Then pick actions and parameters that do not depend on the oximeter.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: Fifteen minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells, a patient reports chills and low back pain. Temperature rose from 36.9 °C to 38.3 °C. What does the nurse do first?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Slow the transfusion and recheck vital signs in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Slowing still delivers incompatible cells. Chills, back pain and a fever early in a transfusion suggest a hemolytic reaction, so the transfusion is stopped, not slowed.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and continue the transfusion as ordered
options.rationale: Near miss concept Treating the fever hides the reaction while more incompatible blood is given.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the IV line open
options.rationale: Stopping limits how much incompatible blood enters. Keeping the line open with 0.9% sodium chloride (new tubing) preserves access for treatment; then the provider and blood bank are notified.

options.text: Send a blood sample for a Coombs test before stopping
options.rationale: Correct but premature A Coombs test helps confirm a hemolytic reaction, but testing never comes before stopping the infusion.

questions.takeaway: Signs of a transfusion reaction mean stop the transfusion first, keep the line open with 0.9% sodium chloride, then notify the provider and blood bank. Typing, antibody screen and crossmatch exist to prevent this reaction.
questions.strategy: Every option except one keeps the blood running or delays stopping it. In a suspected reaction, the first action removes the cause.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: On heparin day 6, a patient's platelets are 98 K/µL, down from 260 K/µL on admission. The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) is in the ordered range. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Continue the infusion because the aPTT is therapeutic
