questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: After starting a daily spinach and kale smoothie, a patient on the same warfarin dose has an international normalized ratio (INR) of 1.5, down from 2.6. How does the nurse interpret this?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: New vitamin K intake is reducing warfarin's effect
options.rationale: Warfarin works by reducing the vitamin K dependent clotting factors. A sudden rise in vitamin K from leafy greens lets the liver make more factors, so the INR falls below goal.

options.text: The patient needs to stop eating leafy greens
options.rationale: Near miss concept Leafy greens do not have to be removed; the teaching is to keep vitamin K intake consistent.

options.text: The INR is in the expected range for warfarin
options.rationale: Near miss concept An INR of 1.5 is below the usual goal of 2 to 3, so the patient is less protected from clots.

options.text: The smoothie is raising the risk of bleeding
options.rationale: Near miss concept More vitamin K pushes toward clotting, not bleeding. A falling INR means less anticoagulant effect.

questions.takeaway: A sudden increase in vitamin K lowers warfarin's effect and the INR. Teach consistent vitamin K intake, not avoidance, and report the change to the provider.
questions.strategy: Link the new habit to how warfarin works: more vitamin K means more clotting factors, which means a lower INR.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient taking warfarin reports black, tarry stools for 2 days and feels lightheaded when standing. The international normalized ratio (INR) is 4.8. Which action does the nurse take first?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Teach the patient to avoid foods high in vitamin K
options.rationale: Near miss concept Vitamin K foods do not cause a high INR, and teaching does not address active bleeding.

options.text: Hold the warfarin dose and notify the provider
options.rationale: Melena with lightheadedness and an INR above goal is active GI bleeding from too much anticoagulant effect. The dose is held and the provider notified so reversal and a hemoglobin can be ordered.

options.text: Give the scheduled warfarin dose and recheck the INR tomorrow
options.rationale: Near miss concept Giving more anticoagulant to a bleeding patient worsens the bleed.

options.text: Collect a stool sample for occult blood testing
options.rationale: Near miss concept The stool is already black and tarry, which is visible blood. Testing for hidden blood delays action.

questions.takeaway: Melena plus an INR above goal on warfarin means active bleeding: hold the dose and notify the provider. Teaching and further testing come later.
questions.strategy: Find the active problem first. Black stools and lightheadedness show the patient is bleeding now, so the action must stop more anticoagulant and get help.

questions.stem: An 83 year old patient is newly confused 2 days after hip surgery. Temperature is 37.7 °C, crackles are present, and white blood cells are 8,400/mm3. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Report the findings as a possible infection
options.rationale: New confusion with crackles and a temperature rise suggests pneumonia. In older adults the WBC count may not rise with infection, so a normal count does not rule it out.

options.text: Document the confusion as expected after surgery in older adults
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem New confusion is a change from baseline, often the first sign of infection in an older adult, and is not assumed to be normal.

options.text: Reassure the family that the normal WBC rules out infection
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem This is the trap: aging blunts the WBC response, so the count can be normal with infection.

options.text: Recheck the temperature in 4 hours before reporting
options.rationale: Near miss concept Waiting delays care when several cues already point to infection.

questions.takeaway: In older adults the WBC count may not rise with infection. New confusion, a temperature rise and focal lung findings are reported even with a normal WBC.
questions.strategy: Weigh the cluster of cues against the one normal lab: the WBC is the unreliable piece in an older adult.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient with type O positive blood is ordered one unit of red blood cells. At the bedside check, the unit is labeled A positive. What does the nurse do?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Hang the unit slowly and stay for 15 minutes
options.rationale: Near miss concept Staying the first 15 minutes is correct for a compatible unit, but this unit is incompatible. Slow infusion still risks a hemolytic reaction.

options.text: Ask the patient whether they have had transfusions before
options.rationale: Near miss concept A transfusion history matters for antibodies, but it does not change the fact that this unit does not match.

options.text: Return the unit to the blood bank unused
options.rationale: An O patient has antibodies against A cells. A mismatched unit is never given; it goes back to the blood bank so the right unit can be issued.

options.text: Give it because both are Rh positive
options.rationale: Near miss concept Rh matching alone is not enough. ABO must also be compatible, and an O patient cannot receive A cells.

questions.takeaway: ABO/Rh typing, antibody screen and crossmatch exist to prevent a transfusion reaction. If the unit does not match at the bedside check, it is not given.
questions.strategy: Check both parts of the type: Rh matches, but ABO does not, and either mismatch stops the transfusion.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected leukemia has left upper abdominal fullness, petechiae on both legs and a platelet count of 34 K/µL. The nurse is observing a nursing student assess a patient with suspected leukemia. For each student action, indicate whether it is appropriate or requires the nurse to intervene.

rows.text: Palpates deeply under the left ribs to feel the spleen
Palpates lymph nodes gently and notes size
Asks about bleeding after brushing teeth
Applies brief pressure, then moves on after a blood draw
Uses a firm, tight blood pressure cuff on the same arm repeatedly
Inspects the skin and gums for bleeding

questions.takeaway: An enlarged spleen ruptures easily. The nurse does not palpate it when a hematologic problem is suspected; the provider assesses it. Gentle lymph node palpation is part of the hematologic assessment; document size, tenderness and whether the node moves. Gum bleeding is a platelet related finding worth asking about. With a known or suspected bleeding problem, pressure is held until the bleeding stops, which can take several minutes. Repeated, prolonged cuff pressure can cause bruising and petechiae with a low platelet count; handle the patient gently. Inspection for petechiae, bruising and gum bleeding is a key part of assessing a patient with low platelets. With a suspected hematologic problem, examine gently, do not palpate the spleen, and hold pressure on puncture sites until bleeding stops.
questions.strategy: For each action ask: could it cause bleeding or rupture in a patient with low platelets and an enlarged spleen?

questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: “I will need to lie still for about an hour during the scan.”
options.rationale: The scan itself takes about an hour of lying still on the table, so the teaching was understood. Extra fluids help flush the tracer out through the urine. Small amounts of tracer can set off airport radiation detectors for several days, so the patient may carry a note.

options.text: “I should keep away from my family for a week afterward.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The tracer dose is small and short lived. No isolation from family is needed after a bone scan.

options.text: “I will drink extra water after the scan.”
options.rationale: The scan itself takes about an hour of lying still on the table, so the teaching was understood. Extra fluids help flush the tracer out through the urine. Small amounts of tracer can set off airport radiation detectors for several days, so the patient may carry a note.

options.text: “The tracer will be given to me as a pill.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The tracer is usually injected IV, then the scan is done after it collects in bone.

options.text: “Airport screening may detect the tracer for a few days.”
options.rationale: The scan itself takes about an hour of lying still on the table, so the teaching was understood. Extra fluids help flush the tracer out through the urine. Small amounts of tracer can set off airport radiation detectors for several days, so the patient may carry a note.

questions.takeaway: A bone scan uses a small IV dose of radioactive tracer: lie still about an hour, drink water afterward, and expect that airport screening may detect it for several days. No isolation is needed.
questions.strategy: Judge each statement as true or false about a diagnostic tracer, which is a small dose that leaves through the urine.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with advanced liver cirrhosis. Which findings does the nurse expect because of the liver's role in blood health? Select all that apply.
questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

options.text: Platelet count above normal
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Platelets are often low in cirrhosis, because an enlarged spleen traps them. A high count is not expected.

options.text: Easy bruising on the arms
options.rationale: The liver makes most clotting factors. With fewer factors, small bumps bruise easily. The INR rises when the liver cannot make enough clotting factors, even without warfarin. Low clotting factors cause oozing from small mucosal injuries like brushing.

options.text: Shortened time for blood to clot
options.rationale: Near miss concept Fewer clotting factors make clotting slower, not faster.

options.text: Prolonged international normalized ratio
options.rationale: The liver makes most clotting factors. With fewer factors, small bumps bruise easily. The INR rises when the liver cannot make enough clotting factors, even without warfarin. Low clotting factors cause oozing from small mucosal injuries like brushing.

options.text: Gums that bleed when brushing teeth
options.rationale: The liver makes most clotting factors. With fewer factors, small bumps bruise easily. The INR rises when the liver cannot make enough clotting factors, even without warfarin. Low clotting factors cause oozing from small mucosal injuries like brushing.

questions.takeaway: The liver makes many plasma proteins and clotting factors. In liver failure, expect bruising, mucosal bleeding and a prolonged INR.
questions.strategy: Start from what the liver makes: clotting factors. Every correct finding is a result of having too few of them.

questions.topic: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms
questions.stem: A patient with a new leg clot started on heparin asks, “Will this dissolve my clot?” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

options.text: “Heparin keeps the clot from growing while your body breaks it down.”
options.rationale: Heparin is an anticoagulant: it stops new fibrin from forming. The body's own fibrinolytic system, through plasmin, dissolves the existing clot over time.

options.text: “Yes, heparin dissolves the clot within the first few hours.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heparin does not break down fibrin. Dissolving a clot quickly takes a fibrinolytic drug such as alteplase.

options.text: “Heparin thins the blood so the clot passes through your veins.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Heparin does not thin the blood or move the clot. A clot that travels is an embolism, which is a danger, not a goal.

options.text: “No, the clot will stay the same size for the rest of your life.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The body's fibrinolytic system breaks clots down over weeks, so the clot usually shrinks.

questions.takeaway: Anticoagulants such as heparin stop new clot formation; they do not dissolve an existing clot. Fibrinolysis, through plasmin, breaks the clot down.
questions.strategy: Separate the two halves of hemostasis: formation and breakdown. Heparin acts on formation only, so any option claiming it dissolves or moves the clot is wrong.

questions.stem: A patient with severe anemia has hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Pale inner eyelids and nail beds
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Pallor is expected with this hemoglobin. It confirms the anemia but is not a new danger.

options.text: Chest pressure while walking to the bathroom
options.rationale: Chest pressure on exertion means the heart is not getting enough oxygen. Low hemoglobin can cause myocardial ischemia, so this needs immediate follow up.

options.text: Fatigue after showering in the morning
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Fatigue is expected with low oxygen carrying capacity. It is planned for, not escalated.

options.text: Cool hands and feeling cold in the room
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Feeling cold is a common, expected finding with anemia.

questions.takeaway: With severe anemia, pallor, fatigue and cold intolerance are expected; chest pain or pressure means the heart is short of oxygen and is escalated right away.
questions.strategy: Every option fits anemia, so ask which one threatens an organ. Chest pressure signals the heart is starved of oxygen.

questions.topic: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests
questions.stem: Two hours after a posterior iliac crest bone marrow biopsy, a patient with platelets of 54 K/µL rates site pain 5 of 10 and asks for ibuprofen. A 2 cm spot on the dressing is unchanged from the last check. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg and heart rate 84/min. Which action is most appropriate?
questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

options.text: Give the prescribed ibuprofen, since the bleeding is controlled
options.rationale: Near miss concept Ibuprofen is an NSAID that impairs platelet function. With platelets already low, it raises the risk of new bleeding at the site even if the spot is stable now.

options.text: Remove the dressing to look directly at the puncture site
options.rationale: Near miss concept Removing the pressure dressing this early can restart bleeding. An unchanged spot is assessed through the dressing.

options.text: Give the prescribed acetaminophen and apply an ice pack
options.rationale: Acetaminophen relieves pain without affecting platelets, and ice reduces bleeding and swelling at the site. The stable spot and normal vital signs show no active bleeding.

options.text: Notify the provider about the drainage on the dressing
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A small spot that has not grown, with normal vital signs, is expected after a biopsy. Calling about it delays the pain relief the patient needs now.

questions.takeaway: After a bone marrow biopsy in a patient with low platelets, avoid NSAIDs and aspirin, keep the pressure dressing on, use ice and a non platelet drug for pain, and watch for a growing stain.
questions.strategy: Two cues decide it: the low platelet count rules out the NSAID, and the unchanged spot with normal vital signs means there is nothing new to report.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient is on day 6 of subcutaneous enoxaparin after a hip replacement. Which result does the nurse report to the provider?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Activated partial thromboplastin time 31 seconds
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Enoxaparin is not monitored with the aPTT, so a normal aPTT is expected and says nothing about the drug's effect.

options.text: Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, down from 12.1 g/dL
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem A drop of 0.3 g/dL after hip surgery is small and expected from postoperative blood loss and fluids. It does not suggest new bleeding.

options.text: International normalized ratio 1.0
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem The INR measures warfarin effect. Enoxaparin does not change it, so a normal INR is expected.

options.text: Platelets 105 K/µL, down from 240 K/µL
options.rationale: A platelet count that falls by more than half 5 to 10 days into heparin or enoxaparin suggests heparin induced thrombocytopenia, which needs prompt report.

questions.takeaway: INR and aPTT do not measure enoxaparin. What is monitored is bleeding, kidney function and the platelet count; a fall of more than half 5 to 10 days in is reported.
questions.strategy: Ask which test actually tracks enoxaparin safety. The two clotting times are normal because the drug does not affect them; the platelet trend is the danger signal.

questions.topic: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities
questions.stem: A patient rescued from a house fire has a headache and is slow to answer questions. Pulse oximetry reads 99% on room air. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

options.text: Apply 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin, and the pulse oximeter reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxygenated, so 99% is falsely reassuring. Headache and confusion after smoke exposure call for high flow oxygen right away.

options.text: Draw an arterial blood gas with carboxyhemoglobin
options.rationale: Near miss concept A carboxyhemoglobin level confirms the poisoning, but it is drawn after oxygen is started. Waiting for the result delays treatment.

options.text: Recheck the oxygen saturation on another finger
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Rechecking at another site gives the same falsely normal value. The problem is the device, not the finger.

options.text: Give acetaminophen for the headache as prescribed
options.rationale: Near miss concept The headache comes from poor oxygen delivery to the brain. Treating the symptom leaves the cause untreated.

questions.takeaway: In suspected carbon monoxide poisoning, a normal pulse oximetry value is not reassuring. Start 100% oxygen by nonrebreather first, then confirm with a carboxyhemoglobin level.
questions.strategy: Weigh the cue against the number: smoke exposure plus headache and confusion outranks a 99% value the device cannot get right.

questions.topic: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health
questions.stem: The occupational health nurse reviews six workers with new blood or oxygen related complaints. For each worker, indicate the environmental exposure the nurse most suspects.
questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

rows.text: Forklift driver in a closed propane warehouse with headaches that ease on weekends
Painter scraping old paint off a 1930s bridge with fatigue and anemia
Refinery worker with bruising, frequent infections and low counts of all blood cells
Home renovator sanding window frames in an older house, with abdominal pain and anemia
Mechanic who runs engines in a closed garage, now with headache and nausea
Gas station attendant with fatigue and a falling platelet count over a year

questions.takeaway: Fuel burning engines indoors produce carbon monoxide. Symptoms that improve away from the site point to an exposure at work. Old paint is a major lead source. Lead blocks heme production, which causes anemia. Benzene damages the bone marrow itself, so every cell line can fall: bleeding, infection and anemia. Sanding releases lead dust. Abdominal pain with anemia is a classic lead picture. Running engines in a closed space builds up carbon monoxide, which binds hemoglobin and starves tissues of oxygen. Gasoline vapor contains benzene, a marrow toxin. A slow fall in counts fits long term exposure. Lead comes from old paint, dust and soil and causes anemia by blocking heme production. Benzene from gasoline and industry harms the marrow, lowering all counts. Carbon monoxide from burning fuel in closed spaces binds hemoglobin.
questions.strategy: Match the source first, then confirm with the blood effect: anemia alone fits lead, all cell lines low fits benzene, headache that clears away from the site fits carbon monoxide.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient on a continuous heparin infusion has an activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) of 118 seconds; the target range is 60 to 80 seconds. The patient has new oozing at an old IV site and the gums bleed with brushing. Blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg and heart rate 88/min. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: Stop the heparin infusion
options.rationale: The aPTT is far above the target and new bleeding has started. Stopping the drug removes the cause, and heparin's short half life means its effect begins to fade within hours.

options.text: Give protamine sulfate as the heparin antidote
options.rationale: Outside the nurse's scope Protamine reverses heparin, but it needs a provider order and is usually saved for serious bleeding. Stopping the infusion comes first and may be enough.

options.text: Recheck the aPTT in 1 hour to confirm the result
options.rationale: Near miss concept Confirming the value while the drug keeps running lets the bleeding worsen. The bleeding already confirms the result.

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the oozing IV site
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pressure helps the site, but the infusion is still delivering the drug that causes bleeding everywhere. Treat the cause first.

questions.takeaway: An aPTT far above target with new bleeding means stop the heparin first, then notify the provider, who may order protamine. Pressure and rechecks come after.
questions.strategy: Every option is reasonable, so ask which one stops the harm at its source. The vital signs are normal, so this is not yet a resuscitation; removing the drug is.

questions.stem: A patient with iron deficiency anemia started oral ferrous sulfate 2 weeks ago. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL. At a clinic visit, the patient reports four concerns. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Heart rate 118/min at rest and dizziness when standing
options.rationale: A fast resting heart rate with dizziness on standing shows the body can no longer compensate for the low hemoglobin. This patient may need a transfusion and an evaluation for ongoing blood loss.

options.text: Stools that have turned dark green to black
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Oral iron commonly darkens stools. Without a tarry texture, lightheadedness or a falling hemoglobin, this is expected.

options.text: A strong craving to chew ice throughout the day
options.rationale: Near miss concept Craving ice, called pica, is a typical sign of iron deficiency. It confirms the diagnosis but is not dangerous.

options.text: Tiredness after climbing one flight of stairs
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Fatigue with exertion is expected at this hemoglobin. It is planned for with rest periods, not escalated.

questions.takeaway: In anemia, pallor, fatigue, pica and dark stools on oral iron are expected. A fast resting heart rate with orthostatic dizziness means compensation is failing and needs follow up now.
questions.strategy: Three options are classic findings of iron deficiency or its treatment. The decision is which one shows the body is decompensating; a trap is the dark stool, which is expected on iron.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a temperature of 37.6 °C. White blood cells are 2,000/mm3 with 20% neutrophils and 5% bands. The patient asks whether visitors can come. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: “Your infection fighting cells are very low, so visitors who are sick must stay away.”
options.rationale: The absolute neutrophil count is 2,000 × (0.20 + 0.05) = 500/mm3, which is severe neutropenia. Visitors are allowed, but anyone with signs of illness should not visit, and everyone performs hand hygiene.

options.text: “Your white count is only mildly low, so normal visiting is fine.”
options.rationale: Absolute language The total count hides the danger. Only neutrophils and bands fight bacteria, and they total 500/mm3, which is severe.

options.text: “No visitors are allowed until your white count returns to normal.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept Banning all visitors is not required and harms the patient's support. Screening visitors for illness and hand hygiene are the protective steps.

options.text: “Visitors can come as long as they wear a mask and you have no fever today.”
options.rationale: Near miss concept The neutrophil count, not the temperature, sets the risk. A patient with severe neutropenia may not mount a fever, and masks alone do not replace excluding ill visitors.

questions.takeaway: Absolute neutrophil count = white cells × (percent neutrophils + percent bands). Below 500/mm3 is severe: screen visitors for illness, enforce hand hygiene and treat any fever as an emergency.
questions.strategy: Do the math before judging: the white count alone looks only mildly low. Then pick the response that protects the patient without needless isolation.

questions.topic: Describe major blood components and their functions
questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has a serum albumin of 2.3 g/dL and new pitting edema in both legs and the abdomen. Blood pressure and heart sounds are unchanged. Which explanation for the edema is most accurate?
questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

options.text: Low albumin lowers the pull that holds fluid in vessels
options.rationale: Albumin, made by the liver, creates oncotic pressure that keeps fluid inside the vessels. With less albumin, fluid leaks into the tissues even without heart failure.

options.text: The heart is failing to pump the extra fluid forward
options.rationale: Near miss concept Unchanged heart sounds and blood pressure do not point to heart failure. The cue is the low albumin.

options.text: Too much sodium is being absorbed from the diet
options.rationale: Near miss concept Sodium can worsen fluid retention, but it does not explain why fluid leaves the vessels here.

options.text: Clotting factors are too low to seal the vessel walls
options.rationale: Near miss concept Clotting factors stop bleeding; they do not hold fluid inside vessels.

questions.takeaway: Albumin is the main plasma protein holding fluid in the vessels by oncotic pressure. Low albumin, as in liver disease or malnutrition, causes edema.
questions.strategy: Link the abnormal lab to its job. Albumin holds water in the vessels, so low albumin lets it escape.

questions.topic: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms
questions.stem: A patient taking warfarin has an INR of 6.4 with no bleeding. Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms
questions.sentence: The nurse expects to [[1]] and anticipates an order for [[2]], because warfarin works by [[3]].

options.text: switch to the evening dose time
hold the next warfarin dose
double the next dose
give the next dose as scheduled
an extra enoxaparin dose
a platelet transfusion
oral vitamin K
protamine sulfate
dissolving existing clots
blocking vitamin K dependent clotting factors
lowering the platelet count
blocking thrombin directly in the blood

questions.takeaway: An INR far above the usual goal of 2 to 3 means the next dose is held and the provider is notified. Without bleeding, a high INR is usually managed by holding warfarin and sometimes giving low dose oral vitamin K. Warfarin blocks the liver's use of vitamin K to make factors 2, 7, 9 and 10, so vitamin K reverses it. Warfarin blocks vitamin K dependent factors 2, 7, 9 and 10. A high INR without bleeding: hold warfarin, notify, and expect oral vitamin K if ordered. Protamine is for heparin.
questions.strategy: Tie the antidote to the mechanism: warfarin blocks vitamin K, so vitamin K reverses it.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses a patient with a dark skin tone and suspected hemolytic anemia. Where does the nurse look to assess most accurately for jaundice?

options.text: The palms and the soles of the feet
options.rationale: Near miss concept Palms and soles can look yellow from calluses or carotene, which misleads.

options.text: The skin of the forearm and chest
options.rationale: Near miss concept Melanin in the skin hides the yellow color of bilirubin.

options.text: The nail beds after pressing on them
options.rationale: Near miss concept Pressing the nail beds checks capillary refill, not jaundice.

options.text: The sclera and the hard palate
options.rationale: In darker skin, yellowing shows best where skin pigment does not mask it: the sclera and the hard palate. Look in natural light.

questions.takeaway: In darker skin, assess jaundice in the sclera and hard palate, pallor in the conjunctivae and mucous membranes, and cyanosis in the lips, tongue and nail beds.
questions.strategy: Choose the site where skin pigment cannot hide the color change.

questions.topic: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes
questions.stem: One week after starting oral iron, a patient's hemoglobin is unchanged at 8.9 g/dL, but the reticulocyte count has risen from 0.4% to 3.5%. The patient asks if the iron is working. Which response is best?
questions.objective: Connect lab tests with clinical purposes

options.text: “No, your hemoglobin should be normal by now.”
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Hemoglobin rises slowly, over weeks to months; no change at 1 week is expected.

options.text: “Yes, your marrow is making new red cells faster.”
options.rationale: A rising reticulocyte count is the earliest sign that iron therapy is working. Hemoglobin follows over the next weeks.

options.text: “It is too early for any test to tell us.”
options.rationale: Absolute language The reticulocyte count already shows a response within days.

options.text: “The rising count means you are losing blood.”
options.rationale: Expected finding offered as a problem Reticulocytes can rise after bleeding, but in a patient starting iron the expected cause is a response to treatment.

questions.takeaway: Reticulocytes are young red cells. A rising count within days of starting iron, B12 or folate shows the marrow is responding; hemoglobin rises later.
questions.strategy: Know which lab moves first: the reticulocyte count, then hemoglobin.

questions.topic: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms
questions.stem: On the second day after a long orthopedic surgery, a patient's D dimer comes back elevated. The patient is resting comfortably, and the nurse is asked what the result means. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.objective: Explain clot formation and breakdown mechanisms

options.text: The patient is deficient in clotting factors and may bleed
options.rationale: Near miss concept An elevated D dimer shows clotting and breakdown are occurring, not a factor deficiency.

options.text: The platelets are being destroyed faster than they are made
options.rationale: Near miss concept Platelet destruction is measured by the platelet count, not the D dimer.

options.text: A clot has formed somewhere and is being broken down
options.rationale: D dimer is a fragment released when fibrin is broken down during fibrinolysis. An elevated level shows that a clot formed and is being dissolved somewhere, but it does not say where. After surgery it is often elevated, so it raises suspicion for a deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism without proving either; imaging confirms.

options.text: The patient has a pulmonary embolism that needs treatment
options.rationale: Label instead of mechanism A D dimer is not specific; a pulmonary embolism is one possible source, not the meaning of the result.

questions.takeaway: High D dimer: a clot is being broken down somewhere.
questions.strategy: Separate what a lab measures from the diagnosis it raises.

questions.topic: Describe major blood components and their functions
questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has oozing gums, bruises on the forearms and pitting edema of both legs. The platelet count is normal. Which explanation best links the findings?
questions.objective: Describe major blood components and their functions

options.text: Portal hypertension forces fluid and blood out of vessels
options.rationale: Near miss concept Portal hypertension causes ascites and varices, but it does not explain gum oozing with a normal platelet count.

options.text: A low red cell count lowers the plasma oncotic pressure
options.rationale: Near miss concept Albumin, not red cells, holds fluid in the vessels.

options.text: The liver makes both clotting factors and albumin
options.rationale: Plasma proteins come from the liver. When the liver fails, clotting factor production falls, so the patient bleeds even with normal platelets, and albumin falls, so oncotic pressure drops and fluid leaks into tissues. One organ explains both findings.

options.text: Low platelets cause both bleeding and capillary leak
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data The platelet count is normal, so platelets do not explain the bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Liver failure: bleeding and edema from missing plasma proteins.
questions.strategy: Use the normal platelet count to rule out the obvious answer.

questions.topic: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities
questions.stem: Three members of one household arrive in winter with headaches and nausea. One is confused, with an oxygen saturation of 99% on room air by pulse oximeter. What should the nurse do first for the confused patient?
questions.objective: Recognize carbon monoxide poisoning and nursing priorities

options.text: Obtain a carboxyhemoglobin level to confirm exposure
options.rationale: Correct but premature The level confirms the diagnosis, but treatment starts on suspicion.

options.text: Recheck the oxygen saturation on a different finger
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data A pulse oximeter reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxygenated hemoglobin; another finger will read the same.

options.text: Perform a full neurological assessment and document it
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting Assessment and documentation delay the treatment that reverses the poisoning.

options.text: Apply 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin far more tightly than oxygen, and a standard pulse oximeter cannot tell the two apart, so the saturation reads falsely normal. A household cluster with headache, nausea and confusion is carbon monoxide until proven otherwise. High flow 100% oxygen shortens the half life of carboxyhemoglobin and is started before the level returns.

questions.takeaway: Suspected carbon monoxide: 100% oxygen now; the oximeter lies.
questions.strategy: Treat on suspicion when the test is slow and the oximeter is unreliable.

questions.topic: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests
questions.stem: Two hours after a posterior iliac crest bone marrow aspiration, a patient with a platelet count of 40,000/mm³ reports throbbing pain at the site. The dressing is dry, but the nurse feels a firm swelling beneath it. What should the nurse do first?
questions.objective: Understand nursing care before and after bone marrow tests

options.text: Give the prescribed acetaminophen for the procedure pain
options.rationale: Correct action, wrong question Treating the pain ignores the cause, a likely hematoma.

options.text: Apply ice and recheck the dressing again in one hour
options.rationale: Correct but premature Ice may help later, but waiting an hour allows bleeding to continue.

options.text: Reinforce the dressing and help the patient lie on the site
options.rationale: Near miss concept A dry dressing hides bleeding into the tissue; reinforcing it treats the wrong problem.

options.text: Apply firm pressure to the site and notify the provider
options.rationale: With a low platelet count, bleeding after the procedure may collect under the skin instead of soaking the dressing. A firm, painful swelling suggests a hematoma. The nurse applies direct pressure to stop the bleeding and reports it, then monitors the site and vital signs.

questions.takeaway: Dry dressing, firm swelling, low platelets: bleeding under the skin.
questions.strategy: Look past the dressing to the finding beneath it.

questions.topic: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health
questions.stem: A patient who restores old houses has fatigue and pallor. The hemoglobin is low and the red cells are small. Which assessment question will be most useful?
questions.objective: Identify environmental exposures affecting blood health

options.text: "Have you noticed black or tarry stools lately?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Blood loss is worth asking about, but it ignores the clue in the history.

options.text: "Does anyone in your family have anemia?"
options.rationale: Accurate but inert data Family history is less useful than a direct exposure clue.

options.text: "Do you sand or scrape old paint at work?"
options.rationale: Lead blocks hemoglobin synthesis and causes a small cell anemia that looks like iron deficiency. Older homes often contain lead paint, and sanding or scraping creates dust. The occupational clue in the stem makes the exposure history the most useful question.

options.text: "How often do you eat red meat or leafy greens?"
options.rationale: Near miss concept Diet fits iron deficiency, but this patient's work points to another cause of small red cells.

questions.takeaway: Small red cells plus old paint: ask about lead.
questions.strategy: Use the history detail the stem gives you.
